templates.title: Occupancy by city and month, with stays that cross month boundaries
templates.subtopic: date ranges split across months, half-open intervals, availability denominators

sections.scenario: A stays marketplace shows hosts and its own market teams how full listings are: of the nights a listing could have been booked, how many were. The report is per city and calendar month, for {{window}}. Hosts block nights they do not want to rent (their own use, repairs), and a blocked night was never on offer, so it must not count against occupancy. Stays are stored as a check-in and a check-out date, and many run across the end of a month, or across the edges of the report window.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns city, month, booked_nights, available_nights, occupancy: one row per city and calendar month inside the window [{{start_date}}, {{end_date}}) that has at least one available night, ordered by city, month. month is the first day of the month, as a DATE. A night is a date; a reservation occupies the nights check_in <= night < check_out, and a block covers start_date <= night < end_date. A night is booked when a reservation with status = 'confirmed' occupies it (cancelled reservations occupy nothing). A night of a listing is available when the listing is listed that night and the night is booked or not blocked. occupancy = booked_nights / available_nights, rounded to 4 decimal places. {{listing_rule}} {{block_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). Confirmed reservations of one listing never overlap each other. Nights outside the window never count, even for a stay that crosses one of its edges. The sample has {{listings}} listings and {{reservations}} reservation rows.
sections.assumptions: Cities, listings, dates and blocks are hypothetical. Dates are the listing's local calendar dates, so there is no time zone to convert. Occupancy can be defined in several ways (over all calendar nights, over available nights, weighted by revenue); this exercise uses booked over available nights, as defined above.
sections.criteria: Thinks in nights with half-open stays and blocks; splits stays across months and clips them to the window; confirmed reservations only; blocked nights out of the denominator, counted once even when blocks overlap; booked nights stay available whatever covers them (Very Hard); listed ranges respected (Hard+); zero-booking months kept; correct rounding and deterministic order; can discuss interval arithmetic at scale, restatements and metric definitions.

clarifications.q: A stay checks in on 30 June and checks out on 3 July. Which months get its nights?
clarifications.a: June gets one night (30 June); July gets two (1 and 2 July). The check-out date is not a night of the stay.

clarifications.q: A city has available nights in a month but no bookings. Is it in the result?
clarifications.a: Yes, with booked_nights 0 and occupancy 0.

clarifications.q: Two blocks cover the same night. Is it blocked twice?
clarifications.a: No. A night is blocked or it is not.

clarifications.q: A listing has every night of a month blocked and nothing booked.
clarifications.a: It adds nothing to that month's available nights. A city-month with no available nights at all has no row.

clarifications.q: How is occupancy rounded?
clarifications.a: ROUND(…, 4) of the exact ratio, half away from zero.

hints: Think in nights, not stays: once you have one row per listing and night, splitting stays across months is just grouping by the night's month.
Build each listing's nights from its listed range clipped to the window (generate_series), then mark every night booked or blocked with EXISTS.
COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE …) gives booked and available nights in one pass; keep the denominator booked OR NOT blocked.
followups: Your night grid has one row per listing per night. For several million listings over a year that is billions of rows. How would you compute the same numbers from interval overlaps instead, without expanding nights?
A reservation is cancelled two months after the stay's month closed, and the report was already sent. Do you restate the past month, and how do the report's readers find out?
Market teams also want occupancy over all calendar nights and revenue-weighted occupancy. How would you name and version these definitions so two dashboards never silently disagree?
A host blocks the whole summer. Should that listing's 0 / 0 months affect the city at all, and how would you stop a few heavily blocked listings from distorting a small city's figure?

rules.ask: How many rows does your night grid have for a year of a market with 50 000 listings, and could you get the same counts from interval overlaps instead?
Which month gets the nights of a stay that checks in on 30 June and checks out on 3 July?
A stay starts five days before the window and ends inside it. How many of its nights does your sum count?
A city has availability in a month but no bookings at all. Does your join keep that row?
Two blocks cover the same night, and a third covers a booked night. How many times does your query subtract each?

templates.title: Refunds owed under this exercise's flexible, moderate and strict cancellation rules
templates.subtopic: rule tables, choosing the applicable tier, timestamp arithmetic, money in integer cents

sections.scenario: On a stays marketplace each host picks a cancellation policy for their listing, and a guest who cancels gets back an amount that depends on the policy and on how much notice they gave. Finance needs, for every cancelled booking, the amount owed back, so it can reconcile what was actually refunded. The policies below are this exercise's own rules, stored in a table (check current docs for any real marketplace's policies): flexible pays 100% of the nightly amount plus the service fee with at least {{flexible_days}} days' notice and 50% otherwise; moderate pays 100% plus the service fee with at least {{moderate_days}} days' notice and {{moderate_pct}}% otherwise; strict pays 50% with at least {{strict_days}} days' notice and nothing otherwise.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns booking_id, policy, days_before, nightly_refund_pct, refund_cents: one row per booking with at least one row in cancellations, ordered by booking_id. days_before is the whole days of notice, floor((check_in − cancelled_at) / 1 day) (negative after check-in). A tier of the booking's policy applies when days_before >= min_notice_days. The booking gets the applicable tier with the highest nightly_refund_pct, reported as nightly_refund_pct. For a cancellation before check_in: refund_cents = nights × nightly_cents × nightly_refund_pct / 100, rounded half up to whole cents, plus cleaning_cents in full, plus service_fee_cents if the tier's service_fee_refunded. {{grace_rule}} {{dup_rule}} {{stay_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). Amounts are integer cents and the result must be exact. Every policy has a tier with min_notice_days = 0 and no booking window, so some tier always applies before check-in; tiers of one policy never share a percentage. All timestamps are UTC.
sections.assumptions: Policies, tiers, prices and fees are hypothetical and much simpler than any real marketplace's rules (no taxes, no currencies, no host-initiated cancellations, no special circumstances). The tier table is the single source of the rules: a correct query keeps working when finance adds a tier.
sections.criteria: One cancellation per booking (the earliest, Hard+); notice in whole days with the boundary inclusive; rules read from the tier table, the most generous applicable tier chosen; the booking-window condition on the grace tier (Hard+); integer money with half-up rounding; cleaning fee and the tier's service fee; mid-stay cancellations refund only nights not begun, at the base tier, without fees (Very Hard); can discuss policy changes, currencies, reconciliation and rule versioning.

clarifications.q: Check-in is at 15:00 on the 20th and the guest cancels at 15:00 on the 13th. How many days of notice?
clarifications.a: Exactly 7, so a 7-day tier applies. At 15:00:01 on the 13th it is 6.

clarifications.q: Is the cleaning fee refunded?
clarifications.a: In full, for any cancellation before check-in.

clarifications.q: How is a half cent rounded?
clarifications.a: Half up: 12 345.5 cents becomes 12 346.

clarifications.q: Several tiers apply. Which one counts?
clarifications.a: The one with the highest nightly_refund_pct; its own service_fee_refunded decides the service fee.

clarifications.q: Should bookings that were never cancelled appear?
clarifications.a: No. Only bookings with at least one cancellation event.

hints: Reduce cancellations to one row per booking first.
Join each booking to every tier of its policy that applies, then keep the most generous one per booking (DISTINCT ON or ROW_NUMBER).
Do the money in integers: (nights * nightly_cents * pct + 50) / 100 rounds half up without floating point.
followups: A host changes the listing's policy after a guest has booked. Which policy should apply, and what would you store on the booking to make this query right?
Guests pay in many currencies, and a refund paid a week later meets a different exchange rate. In which currency is the amount owed fixed, and where?
Support also issues partial refunds and goodwill credits on top of the policy. How would you model refunds so finance can reconcile owed against paid, booking by booking?
The rules themselves change (a new tier for long stays next quarter). How would you version policy_tiers so last year's refunds can be recomputed exactly?

rules.ask: A booking has two cancellation events: a retry logged later with an earlier timestamp. Which one decides the notice, and how does your query pick it?
Where in your arithmetic can a half cent appear, which way must it round, and could floating point move it?
Your tiers are written into a CASE expression. What happens next quarter when finance adds a tier to the table?
The guest cancels at 23:00 on the 13th for a 15:00 check-in on the 20th. How many whole days of notice does your expression give?

templates.title: Host response time: median minutes to the first real reply
templates.subtopic: first qualifying event per thread, medians with PERCENTILE_CONT, denominators with unanswered rows

sections.scenario: Guests often message a host before booking, and how quickly hosts answer shapes whether the guest books at all. The marketplace shows hosts their own response time and the share of inquiries they answered within a day. The message log is noisy: hosts can turn on automated replies that fire within seconds, guests send follow-ups before anyone answers, and support sometimes joins a thread. None of those is a host answering.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns host_id, inquiries, answered, within_24h, share_within_24h, median_response_minutes, one row per host, ordered by host_id. An inquiry's first reply is the earliest message on that inquiry with is_automated = false sent by the inquiry's host side. Its response time is sent_at − created_at in minutes (whole minutes in this data). answered counts inquiries with a first reply; within_24h counts those answered within 1440 minutes, inclusive; share_within_24h = within_24h / inquiries, rounded to 4 places. median_response_minutes is the median response time over answered inquiries (the average of the two middle values when their number is even), as a numeric rounded to 1 decimal place, or NULL when none was answered. {{scope_rule}} {{host_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). The guest's opening message is in messages too, sent at created_at by the guest. A host can reply several times; only the first real reply counts.
sections.assumptions: Hosts, guests, inquiries and timings are hypothetical. The definition of response time here (clock minutes, no pause overnight, first non-automated host-side message) is this exercise's; a production metric would document its own.
sections.criteria: First reply restricted to the host side and non-automated messages, filtered before the minimum; unanswered inquiries kept in counts and the denominator; 24 hours inclusive; a true median with the even case averaged; the reporting window on created_at with late replies still counting and the minimum-inquiries floor (Hard+); co-host replies credited to the listing's host (Very Hard); can discuss time zones, late data and incremental computation.

clarifications.q: The host's automated reply arrives in 30 seconds and the host writes personally 3 hours later. What is the response time?
clarifications.a: 180 minutes. Automated messages are never replies, even when sent from the host's account.

clarifications.q: Does a reply at exactly 24 hours count as within 24 hours?
clarifications.a: Yes. 1440 minutes is within.

clarifications.q: Do unanswered inquiries count?
clarifications.a: In inquiries and in the share's denominator, yes. They have no response time, so they are not in the median.

clarifications.q: Four answered inquiries took 10, 20, 40 and 300 minutes. What is the median?
clarifications.a: 30.0, the average of 20 and 40 (PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5)).

clarifications.q: A reply is sent after the reporting window ends. Does it count?
clarifications.a: Yes. The window selects inquiries by created_at; replies count whenever they came.

hints: Compute one row per inquiry first: its host and the time of its first qualifying reply (NULL if none). A LEFT JOIN keeps the unanswered ones.
MIN(sent_at) over the qualifying messages is the first reply; filter the messages before taking the minimum, not after.
PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY minutes) ignores NULLs, which is exactly what the median needs.
followups: An inquiry arrives at 3 a.m. in the host's time zone. Should the clock pause overnight, and what would that do to the metric's meaning and its computation?
Phones send messages late when they were offline. Which timestamp would you trust for sent_at, and how would you restate a host's figure when late messages arrive?
This must refresh daily for millions of hosts. What state per open inquiry lets you update it incrementally instead of rescanning every message?
A guest books instantly a minute after asking, and the host never replies. Should that inquiry count against the host, and how would you encode the decision?

rules.ask: Two inquiries were answered in 5 minutes and one in three days. What do the mean and the median say, and which describes a typical guest's wait?
With an even number of answered inquiries, which value does PERCENTILE_DISC return, and does it match the definition here?
Does your first message skip the guest's own follow-ups and the automated replies before the minimum is taken?
An inquiry was never answered. Is it still in your inquiries count and the share's denominator?
Which of your counts includes unanswered inquiries, and which does not?

templates.title: Orphan nights: calendar gaps shorter than the minimum stay
templates.subtopic: sort, merge and scan per key, gaps between occupied runs

sections.scenario: A host sets a minimum stay, say three nights. When two bookings leave a two-night hole between them, nobody can ever book it: an orphan gap. Pricing tools suggest relaxing the minimum stay or discounting exactly those nights, so they first need every orphan gap of every listing, computed nightly across the whole calendar.
sections.problem: Implement orphan_gaps(min_stay, bookings, blocks). min_stay maps each listing id to its minimum stay in nights (at least 1). bookings holds (listing_id, check_in, check_out, status), occupying the nights check_in <= n < check_out; nights are integers (day numbers). blocks holds (listing_id, start, end) in the same half-open form. A listing's occupied nights form runs; a gap is the free nights between two consecutive runs, and it is orphan when 0 < length < min_stay[listing]. Free nights before the first run or after the last are never a gap. Return {listing_id: [(gap_start, gap_end), ...]} for every listing in min_stay, each list sorted by gap_start and holding half-open ranges; a listing with no orphan gap maps to []. {{status_rule}} {{block_rule}} {{order_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 4 000 listings with 100 or more bookings each, calendars of several hundred nights. Checking every booking for every night of every calendar is too slow; aim for O(n log n) in the number of bookings and blocks.
sections.assumptions: Listings, minimum stays and calendars are hypothetical. Minimum stay is one number per listing here; real products let it vary by date and by check-in day.
sections.criteria: Groups by listing and sorts once per group; merges overlapping and touching intervals with a running maximum end; gaps only between runs, with 0 < length < min_stay; half-open arithmetic without off-by-one; cancelled bookings ignored (Hard+); blocks merged with bookings and unknown listings ignored (Very Hard); every listing present in the output; O(n log n) argued; sensible incremental and batch designs.

clarifications.q: Two bookings are back to back (one checks out on the day the next checks in). Is there a gap?
clarifications.a: No. The gap has length 0.

clarifications.q: The minimum stay is 3 and the gap is exactly 3 nights. Orphan?
clarifications.a: No. Somebody can book it. Only gaps shorter than the minimum.

clarifications.q: What about the free nights before the first booking?
clarifications.a: Never a gap: they are not between two runs.

clarifications.q: What is the length of the gap (5, 7)?
clarifications.a: Two nights, 5 and 6.

clarifications.q: Can I return listings in any order?
clarifications.a: Yes; it is a dict. The gaps inside each list must be sorted.

hints: Group the intervals by listing, then sort each group by start.
Walk the sorted intervals keeping the end of the current occupied run; an interval that starts after it opens a gap, and the run's end is the maximum end seen so far, not the last interval's end.
A nested interval (a short booking inside a long block) must not move the run's end backwards.
followups: Minimum stay varies by date (longer in summer) and by check-in weekday. Which minimum applies to a gap, and what changes in your scan?
The calendar changes all day as bookings arrive and cancel. How would you update the orphan gaps of one listing incrementally rather than recomputing it?
As a batch job over every listing on the platform, where would this run, and how would you partition it so one huge listing group does not dominate?
Suppose the pricing tool discounts orphan nights. How would you measure whether that sold nights that would otherwise stay empty, rather than discounting nights that would have sold anyway?

rules.ask: How many night-by-booking checks is that for 4 000 listings with 100 bookings over 700 nights each?
Marking nights works. What does it cost in memory and time when a calendar spans two years, and what does sorting intervals cost instead?
A short booking sits entirely inside a long host block. What does your previous-end variable hold after it?
What exactly do you sort, by which key, and how many separate sorts does the whole run do?

templates.title: Map search across the antimeridian, sorted by price and paged
templates.subtopic: grid buckets, longitude wrap-around, sort and paginate

sections.scenario: Guests search a stays marketplace by dragging a map: every pan or zoom sends the visible rectangle, and the result list shows the listings inside it, cheapest first, a page at a time. Most viewports are small, over one city, but some sit over Fiji or the Chukotka coast, where the map's west edge is at +179° and its east edge at −179°: the viewport crosses the antimeridian, and a naive "west ≤ longitude ≤ east" test finds nothing.
sections.problem: Implement search_map(listings, queries). Each listing is (listing_id, lat, lng, nightly_price) with lng in [−180, 180) and an integer price. Each query is (south, west, north, east, page, page_size, max_price). A listing matches when south <= lat <= north and its longitude is inside the viewport: if west <= east, west <= lng <= east; if west > east, the viewport crosses the antimeridian and lng >= west or lng <= east. Matches are sorted by nightly_price, then listing_id; page is 0-based. For each query return (total_matches, ids) where ids are the listing ids on that page (empty past the end). Return one tuple per query, in order. {{invalid_rule}} {{price_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 60 000 listings and 6 000 queries per call, nearly all viewports a fraction of a degree across. Testing every listing for every query is too slow; build an index once and make each query's work depend on the listings near its viewport.
sections.assumptions: Listings, prices and coordinates are hypothetical. Latitude and longitude are treated as a flat rectangle grid; real map search projects coordinates, ranks by more than price and returns pins and a list separately.
sections.criteria: Inclusive bounds; correct wrap-around when west > east, including longitude −180; sorting by price then id and 0-based paging with the total; the sentinel (0, []) for invalid queries (Hard+); max_price inclusive (Very Hard); an index built once with per-query work proportional to nearby listings, and exact filtering of candidates; can discuss density-adaptive indexes, caching and cursor paging.

clarifications.q: Are the edges of the viewport inclusive?
clarifications.a: Yes, all four.

clarifications.q: How do I know a viewport crosses the antimeridian?
clarifications.a: west > east. A viewport with west == east is one meridian wide.

clarifications.q: Two listings have the same price.
clarifications.a: The smaller listing_id, compared as a string, comes first.

clarifications.q: The page is past the last match.
clarifications.a: Return the total and an empty list.

clarifications.q: Does each query get its own result even when two are identical?
clarifications.a: Yes. One tuple per query, in order.

hints: Bucket listings into grid cells of a fixed size (a fraction of a degree) keyed by (floor(lat / size), floor(lng / size)), once.
A viewport touches a rectangle of cells; one that crosses the antimeridian touches two column ranges, from west to the last column and from the first column to east.
Cells only give candidates: test each candidate exactly against the viewport before sorting. If a viewport would touch more cells than exist, loop over the occupied cells instead.
followups: Listing density varies by orders of magnitude between a city centre and the countryside. How would you choose cell sizes, or switch to a structure that adapts (a quadtree, geohash prefixes)?
Most map moves are small pans. How would you reuse the previous viewport's work, and what would you cache?
Price is the nightly price, but guests see the total for their dates. How does sorting by a date-dependent total change the index and the paging?
Deep pages are rare but expensive. How would cursor-based paging (after the last price and id seen) compare with page numbers when listings change between requests?

rules.ask: How many coordinate checks is that for 6 000 viewports over 60 000 listings?
A viewport has west = 179.5 and east = −179.5. What does your condition return for a listing at longitude 179.9?
The viewport is a rectangle in latitude and longitude. Does a distance from its centre select the same listings?
A new listing appears between a guest's page 1 and page 2. What happens to the listing that was last on page 1?
What does your tree do with a viewport that crosses the antimeridian?

templates.title: Split stays — two listings, one move, every pair that covers the trip
templates.subtopic: free-run arrays, counting intersecting intervals with binary search

sections.scenario: A guest searches for a week in a busy town, and no single listing is free for every night. A stays marketplace can still offer a split stay: the guest stays in one listing for the first part of the trip, moves once, and stays in a second listing for the rest. Before the search page decides whether to show a split-stay section, it needs to know how many pairs of listings could host each searched date range. The calculation runs for every search, over every listing in the map area, so it has to be fast.
sections.problem: Implement split_stays(calendars, queries, min_nights=None, capacity=None, exclude_whole=False). calendars maps a listing id to a string with one character per night of a shared horizon: '.' is free, 'b' is booked and 'x' is blocked by the host. Only '.' is free. Each query is (check_in, check_out, guests) and asks for nights check_in to check_out − 1, with 0 ≤ check_in < check_out ≤ the horizon. A split stay is an ordered pair (first, second) of two different listings and a move night k, with check_in < k < check_out, such that first is free on nights check_in … k − 1 and second is free on nights k … check_out − 1. For each query, return the number of ordered pairs for which at least one move night works; a pair counts once, however many move nights work for it. A one-night query has no move night, so it returns 0. {{min_rule}} {{whole_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 3 000 listings, a horizon of 180 nights and 200 queries per call, with stays of up to a few weeks. Something close to O(n · h) preparation and O(n log n) per query is expected, for n listings and a horizon of h nights. Trying every pair is 9 million pairs per query, which is far too slow.
sections.assumptions: Listings, calendars and searches are hypothetical. Every calendar has the same length. The guest moves exactly once, and the move happens on the morning of night k: the first listing's check-out day is the second listing's check-in day.
sections.criteria: Correct counts with ordered pairs counted once each; one-night queries return 0; booked and blocked nights both unavailable; free-run arrays in each direction; each listing reduced to an interval of acceptable move nights per role; intersecting intervals counted as all pairs minus disjoint ones, minus self-pairs; minimum stays applied to both halves and capacity to both listings (Hard); whole-stay hosts removed per query (Very Hard); a clear complexity argument; sensible answers on cheapest pairs, distance and incremental updates.

clarifications.q: Is (A, B) the same pair as (B, A)?
clarifications.a: No. The guest starts in the first listing, so order matters, and both can count.

clarifications.q: If a pair works with three different move nights, does it count three times?
clarifications.a: No. It counts once.

clarifications.q: Does the check-out night have to be free?
clarifications.a: No. The stay is nights check_in to check_out − 1. The move night k is the first night in the second listing.

clarifications.q: Is a host-blocked night different from a booked one here?
clarifications.a: No. Both are unavailable; only '.' is free.

clarifications.q: Can one listing be both halves?
clarifications.a: No. That would not be a move.

clarifications.q: Can a query be invalid?
clarifications.a: No. Every query satisfies 0 ≤ check_in < check_out ≤ the horizon. A one-night query returns 0.

hints: For one query, the first listing matters only through how many nights in a row it is free starting at check_in. The second listing matters only through how many nights in a row it is free ending at check_out − 1.

Precompute, per listing, the length of the free run that starts at each night and the one that ends just before each night. Then each listing gives an interval of move nights it accepts as the first half, and another interval as the second half.
Pairs whose intervals intersect are all pairs minus the disjoint ones. Sorted endpoints and binary search count the disjoint ones in O(n log n). Then remove each listing that would pair with itself.
followups: The page wants the 20 cheapest split stays, where the price is the first listing's nightly price times its nights plus the second's. For one pair the best move night is at an end of its interval. How would you find the 20 cheapest without enumerating all pairs?
Guests prefer two listings close to each other. Add a maximum distance between the halves. What changes in your counting, and what index would you add?
Calendars change thousands of times a minute. What do you keep precomputed, and what do you update when one night is booked?
Allow two moves, so three listings. How does the counting change, and how fast does the number of combinations grow?

rules.ask: How many pairs is that for 3 000 listings, and how many searches a second could one machine serve with it?
Which endpoints did you sort, and how do you make sure a listing is never counted as a pair with itself?
With minimum stays, is the latest possible move night always the one to try? Give a pair where it fails and an earlier move night works.
A listing is free for 40 nights from check-in on a 6-night search. What do you store for it, and how does exclude_whole treat it?
Your precomputed runs go stale when one night is booked. Which entries change, and how many?

templates.title: Forward occupancy curve for every listing and date
templates.subtopic: difference arrays, sliding windows over calendars

sections.scenario: Hosts and pricing tools look at a forward occupancy curve: for each date, how much of the following weeks is already booked. A curve that is high in three weeks' time but low next week tells a host where a price change or a shorter minimum stay might help. The curve is computed from a calendar snapshot for every listing in a market, for every date in a reporting range, and it is recomputed often.
sections.problem: Implement forward_occupancy(listings, bookings, start, end, window=30, blocked=None). Days are integers (day numbers from a fixed epoch). bookings is a list of (listing_id, check_in, check_out, status) and covers nights check_in to check_out − 1. For every listing in listings and every date t from start to end − 1, compute the share of nights t … t + window − 1 that are booked: booked nights divided by available nights in that window, rounded with round(x, 4). Return a dict from each listing id in listings to its list of end − start shares, in date order. Bookings for a listing that is not in listings are ignored. {{block_rule}} {{status_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 2 500 listings, 420 dates, a window of up to 150 nights and a few hundred thousand bookings. start < end. Bookings are not sorted, and they can start before start or end after the last window. Something close to O(B + n · (D + w)) is expected, for B bookings, n listings, D dates and a window of w nights. Rescanning each window night by night is about 160 million checks at the largest size, which is too slow.
sections.assumptions: Listings, bookings, blocks and day numbers are hypothetical. Every listing is active for the whole range. The curve uses one calendar snapshot; when each booking was made does not matter here.
sections.criteria: Correct shares with half-open bookings and windows that start on t; bookings clamped to the range; unknown listings ignored; a listing with no bookings reported as 0, not missing; blocked nights removed from the denominator only when they are not booked, and None when nothing is available (Hard); cancelled bookings ignored and overlapping nights counted once (Very Hard); difference arrays and prefix sums with a clear O(B + n · (D + w)) argument; sensible answers on as-of curves, warehouse formulations and market aggregation.

clarifications.q: Does the window include date t itself?
clarifications.a: Yes. It is nights t to t + window − 1.

clarifications.q: Is the check-out day a booked night?
clarifications.a: No. A booking covers check_in to check_out − 1, so the next guest can check in that day.

clarifications.q: What if the window runs past every booking?
clarifications.a: Those nights are not booked. They still count as available unless they are blocked.

clarifications.q: Should the output be in the order of listings?
clarifications.a: The result is a dict, so key order does not matter. Each list must be in date order.

clarifications.q: Can a booking have check_out <= check_in?
clarifications.a: No. Every booking has at least one night.

hints: Add +1 at a booking's check-in and −1 at its check-out on a per-listing array. A running sum then says whether each night is booked.
Only nights from start to end − 2 + window matter. Clamp every booking and block to that range.
With prefix sums of booked nights and of unavailable nights, every window is two subtractions.
When bookings can overlap, it is whether the running count is above zero, not the count itself, that marks a booked night.
followups: Hosts want the curve as it looked on each past date, using only bookings made by then, to compare their booking pace with last year's. What extra data do you need, and how does the algorithm change?

The curve is needed nightly for millions of listings in a warehouse. Write the idea in SQL or Spark: a nights table with window functions, or an exploded range joined to a date spine. What does each cost?
A market-level curve is wanted. Is it the average of the listings' shares, or total booked nights over total available nights? Which one would a pricing tool want, and why do they differ?
One new booking arrives. Which dates' values change, for which listings, and how would you update only those?

rules.ask: How many night checks is that for 2 500 listings, 420 dates and a 150-night window?
Two confirmed bookings overlap after a sync problem. What does your running sum hold on those nights, and what do you store in the prefix array?
A set of every booked night is fine for lookups. Do you still rescan each window, and what does that cost at the largest size?
What does 0 tell a host that None does not, and how should a market average treat a listing whose value is None?
Your rolling sum needs every night present. How do you build the nightly series from bookings without a row per night per listing?

templates.title: Debug the host payout calculator
templates.subtopic: rounding modes, payout schedules, partial refunds, aggregation keys

sections.scenario: A stays marketplace pays hosts after their guests check in. In this exercise, a short stay is paid in one payout the day after check-in, and a stay of 28 nights or more is paid month by month. A guest who leaves a stay early may be refunded some nights after a cancellation. The marketplace keeps a host service fee of {{fee_pct}} of each payout. Host support has collected complaints about one calculator. Two hosts whose guests checked in on the same day say one of them received both payouts and the other nothing. Some payouts are a cent short. A long-stay host's first monthly payout was too small after a guest left early, and the next one too large. Hosts lose their cleaning fee after a partial refund. Hosts with 60-night stays see a transfer of $0.00 a month after their last real payout. The calculator below is the suspect.
sections.problem:
Fix host_payouts(bookings, fee_bps) so that it meets this specification. Here fee_bps is {{fee_bps}}. {{replay_rule}}

  1. Bookings. Each booking is {"id", "host", "check_in", "nights", "rate", "cleaning", "refund_nights"}. Days are integer day numbers. rate (per night) and cleaning are integer cents. refund_nights is between 0 and nights.
  2. Refunds. The refunded nights are the last refund_nights nights of the stay, and the host is not paid for them. If every night is refunded, the cleaning fee is refunded too and the booking has no payout at all. Otherwise the host keeps the cleaning fee.
  3. Schedule. A stay of fewer than 28 booked nights has one payout on day check_in + 1, covering every paid night and the cleaning fee. A stay of 28 booked nights or more is paid monthly: night i of the stay (counting from 0) belongs to period i // 30, and period p is paid on day check_in + 30·p + 1. The cleaning fee belongs to period 0. A period with no paid night has no payout. Whether a stay is monthly depends on its booked nights, not on its paid nights.
  4. Fee. A payout's gross is its paid nights times rate, plus the cleaning fee when it is in that payout. The host fee is gross × fee_bps / 10000, rounded to the nearest cent with exact halves rounded up, computed for each payout separately. The payout amount is gross minus fee.
  5. Transfers. All payouts to the same host on the same day are added into one transfer. Return a list of [day, host, amount], sorted by day and then by host. A transfer of 0 never appears.
sections.constraints: Keep the function's shape and output format. Up to 100 000 bookings, processed in linear time. Use integer arithmetic for money.
sections.assumptions: These schedule, fee and refund rules are this exercise's own and are simplified; real payout timing, fees and refund terms vary by product, country and policy, so check current docs. All amounts and ids are hypothetical. Taxes, currencies and payout methods are out of scope.
sections.criteria: Finds and explains every bug with its host-facing symptom; transfers keyed by host and day; fees rounded half up with integer arithmetic; refunded nights removed from the end of a long stay; the cleaning fee kept on a partial refund and refunded only with every night; no payout for an empty period; fixes that stay minimal and linear; a test per bug.

clarifications.q: Which nights are refunded, the first or the last?
clarifications.a: The last ones. The guest left early.

clarifications.q: Is a 40-night stay with 15 nights refunded still monthly?
clarifications.a: Yes. The schedule depends on booked nights.

clarifications.q: What is half a cent of fee?
clarifications.a: It rounds up: a fee of 4.5 cents is 5 cents, and so is 5.5 cents rounded to 6.

clarifications.q: Can a transfer be 0?
clarifications.a: No. A period with no paid night has no payout, and a fully refunded stay has none.

clarifications.q: How many bugs are there?
clarifications.a: Several, of different kinds. Each check points at one of them.

hints: Trace a 60-night stay with no refund. How many periods does the loop create, and what does the last one pay?
What does Python's round(4.5) return? And round(5.5)?
Draw nights 0 to 39 of a stay with 5 nights refunded. Which nights does paid_here count in each period?
Look at the key of the transfers dict. What identifies a transfer?
followups: A refund is issued after the first monthly payout was already released. What do you record, and how is the amount recovered from the host?
The payout run crashes halfway and is restarted. How do you make sure no host is paid twice? Name the key you would use.
Hosts are in many time zones. Which calendar decides the payout day, and what changes if it is the host's?
Finance proposes rounding the fee once per transfer instead of once per payout. Who gains, by how much at most, and how would you show it?

rules.ask: Which rounding mode does Python's round use, and where else in a payments codebase would you look for the same mistake?
Would Decimal with ROUND_HALF_UP fix this on its own? What does dividing a float before rounding do to very large amounts?
Is the right number of periods enough, or can a period inside the stay still have no paid night?
A host has listings paid in two currencies. Is (day, host) still the right key for a transfer?
Which key makes one payout safe to send twice: the booking, the period, or the transfer? Why?

templates.title: One calendar from many writers — the host app, channel managers and imported calendars
templates.subtopic: availability as a source of truth, conditional writes, polled external feeds, reconciliation

sections.scenario: A stays marketplace has {{listings}} active listings. Hosts change availability in three ways: in the marketplace's own host app; through channel managers, software-connected tools that manage a host's listings on several sites through an API; and by importing calendar feeds from other sites they list on. About {{external_share}} of listings use a channel manager or an imported calendar. In this exercise, imported feeds are fetched {{import_refresh}}, and the marketplace also exports a feed of its own bookings for other sites to import. Availability writes, bookings included, peak at {{peak_writes}}. Hosts complain about double bookings: two guests with the same nights, one booked here and one booked elsewhere, or two booked here through different routes.
sections.problem: Design the availability system. Cover the source of truth for each listing-night and its states (free, held, booked, blocked by the host, blocked by an import); how a booking request takes its nights atomically; how writes from the host app, the channel-manager API and imported feeds are applied, with ordering, retries and conflicts; how the search index and the exported feed learn about changes; how a double booking that still happens, because an imported feed was stale, is detected and resolved; and the metrics that show which route causes conflicts.
sections.constraints: Two confirmed stays made here must never overlap. Imported feeds can be stale for up to {{import_refresh}}, and they carry only date ranges with an event identifier, not guests or prices. Channel managers retry and can deliver updates out of order. A booking request must be answered within a second. Search may lag by a few seconds but must not show booked nights as free for long.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, intervals and rules are hypothetical. Nights are half-open: a check-out day can be the next guest's check-in day. A booking request that needs the host's approval holds its nights for up to 24 hours in this exercise. Each channel manager sends either full snapshots of a date range or individual changes, with its own timestamps.
sections.criteria: A clear source of truth per listing-night with explicit states; atomic, conditional booking writes over a whole range; request holds that expire safely; imported blocks kept as a separate, diffed layer; idempotent, ordered external writes with versions rather than arrival order; a host block refused over a confirmed booking; change events that keep search and the exported feed fresh; conflict detection with a resolution workflow and a route recorded on each conflict; metrics per route; a plan for each incident.

clarifications.q: Is the marketplace the source of truth for nights booked elsewhere?
clarifications.a: No. It learns about them only through imports or channel managers. It is the source of truth for bookings made on it.

clarifications.q: Can a host block a night that is already booked here?
clarifications.a: No. The write is refused, and the host is told why.

clarifications.q: What happens to an import that says a night is busy when we already have a confirmed booking for it?
clarifications.a: That is a conflict to record and resolve. Neither side is silently overwritten.

clarifications.q: Do channel managers send deltas or snapshots?
clarifications.a: Both kinds exist. Your design should handle both.

clarifications.q: How fresh must the exported feed be?
clarifications.a: As fresh as you can make it, because other sites poll it on their own schedule.

hints: Store availability per listing and night, with a version per listing. Make every booking a conditional write over its whole range, so that two requests for overlapping nights cannot both succeed.
Keep imported blocks as their own layer, keyed by feed and event identifier, and apply each fetch as a diff against the last one. Do not mix them into host blocks.
Make every external write idempotent and ordered per listing: a sequence number or a version you compare, never the arrival order.
followups: A guest books here while an imported feed still shows the nights free; ten minutes later the other site confirms its own guest for the same nights. Who learns about the conflict first, how fast, and what happens to each guest?
A channel manager retries a batch after a timeout, and an older snapshot of a date range arrives after a newer one. Walk through what your system stores.
How would you shrink the exposure window for listings that use imported calendars, without fetching every feed every minute?
Measure it: what is the double-booking rate per route, and how would you show hosts which of their connections causes conflicts?

rules.ask: What exactly does your lock cover: a listing, a night or a range? What happens to a 90-night request while hundreds of 2-night requests for the same listing arrive?
How does that constraint treat a 24-hour request hold that expires, and nights blocked by an import?
The cache says a night is free and the database says it is booked. Which one wins at booking time, and which one does search use?
With imports fetched {{import_refresh}}, what is your exposure window, and how would you shorten it for listings in high demand?
Whose clock does the timestamp come from, and what happens when a channel manager's clock is five minutes behind?

incidents: A popular calendar provider slows down, and fetches of imported feeds, normally done {{import_refresh}}, fall an hour behind for a whole region; double bookings in that region rise the same evening.
A channel manager deploys a bug and sends full-year snapshots marking every night free for 3 000 listings, including nights booked here.
The search index misses a batch of availability changes after a consumer restart, and booked nights appear as free for twenty minutes.

templates.title: Cancellations and refunds, by booking date and by stay date
templates.subtopic: booking lifecycle events, night-level facts, restatement, two reporting grains

sections.scenario: A stays marketplace takes about {{bookings_per_day}} bookings a day in {{currencies}} currencies, made {{booking_window}} before check-in. Each listing has one of {{policies}} cancellation policies that this exercise defines (for example its own flexible, moderate and strict rules), which set the refund by how many days before check-in the guest cancels. Guests and hosts can also alter a booking: change its dates, its number of guests or its price. Two teams ask for the same numbers in different shapes. The marketplace-health team wants cancellation rates by booking date: of the bookings made in a week, how many were later cancelled and how much was refunded. The finance and host-insights teams want the same events by stay date: how many booked nights in a month were lost to cancellations, and the revenue that went with them.
sections.problem: Design the data model and the pipeline that produce both views from the same facts. Cover the source events (booking created, altered, cancelled, refunded) and how they land; how a booking's history is kept so that any past state can be rebuilt; a night-level fact and how alterations move nights between dates; how refunds that arrive later or in parts are attached; how the cancellation policy in force at booking time is recorded; currencies; how a late event restates past reporting periods and what each team sees when it does; and metric definitions that let the two views reconcile.
sections.constraints: A booking can be altered several times and then cancelled; a refund can be partial and can arrive days after the cancellation. Events can arrive late or twice. A report for a closed month may change only through a recorded restatement. The two views must agree on totals over any range that covers both all booking dates and all stay dates of the bookings involved.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, policies and rules are hypothetical; cancellation and refund policies are defined by the exercise and are not quoted from any current policy. Every event carries a booking id, an event id, an event time and the amount in the booking's currency in minor units. Daily exchange rates are available.
sections.criteria: An append-only event log with idempotent landing; a versioned booking state with valid times; a night-level fact that alterations update by ending and starting rows; refunds attached by booking and event, partial and late; the policy recorded at booking time; explicit metric grains and denominators for each view, and a reconciliation between them; restatements of closed periods recorded and explained; a deliberate currency rule; protection against leakage for model training; a plan for each incident.

clarifications.q: Is a booking whose dates were altered a new booking?
clarifications.a: No. It keeps its id and its booking date. Its nights move.

clarifications.q: Does a cancellation always refund everything?
clarifications.a: No. The refund depends on the policy recorded at booking time and on when the guest cancelled, and it can be partial.

clarifications.q: Which date is the booking date of an altered booking?
clarifications.a: The date it was first made. The alteration has its own event date.

clarifications.q: What does the stay-date view count for a booking cancelled after check-in?
clarifications.a: The nights not stayed, which this exercise treats as the last nights of the stay.

clarifications.q: Are host cancellations in scope?
clarifications.a: Yes, as a separate reason: the guest is refunded in full and the host's record is affected.

hints: Keep an append-only event log per booking, and build a versioned booking-state table from it, with valid-from and valid-to times, so any past state can be rebuilt.
A night-level fact (one row per booking and stay night, with its amount and status) answers stay-date questions directly. An alteration ends some rows and starts others.
Decide the grain of each metric before the table: "cancelled bookings by booking week" and "nights lost by stay month" need different denominators.
followups: A refund for a booking made six weeks ago arrives today. Which partitions of each view change, and what does each team see?
A booking is shortened from 7 nights to 4, then cancelled. Walk through the night rows and the refund at each step.
Rates are reported in one currency. Which day's rate do you use for a refund made 60 days after the booking, and why might the two views disagree because of it?
Data science wants to train a cancellation model on this data. What must they not read from your tables to avoid leaking the future into training rows?

rules.ask: A booking is altered twice in one day. What does a daily snapshot miss, and does it matter for either view?
An alteration event arrives two days late. Which versions do you close and reopen, and what does a report run yesterday now show?
At {{bookings_per_day}} bookings a day made {{booking_window}} ahead, how many night rows exist at once, and how do you partition them?
Finance closed last month. How do you change a number in it without losing the version they already reported?
Do you convert at the booking date, the cancellation date or the refund date? What does each choice do to a cancellation rate measured in money?

incidents: A payments outage delays refund events in 3 of the {{currencies}} currencies by four days; the by-booking-date view shows refund amounts dropping and then jumping back.
A bug in the alteration service sends every date change twice, a minute apart, with different event ids.
A policy is renamed in the listing settings and every booking made under its old name loses its policy in the night-level fact.

templates.title: Booking alterations — dates, guests, price differences and who agreed to what
templates.subtopic: reservation versions, alteration requests, price deltas, payment and payout adjustments

sections.scenario: Guests book about {{daily_bookings}} stays a day, and about {{alteration_share}} of reservations are later altered: new dates, a different number of guests, occasionally a different listing from the same host. Either side can propose a change. In this exercise's rules a guest's request must be accepted by the host, a host's proposal must be accepted by the guest, and an unanswered request expires after {{response_hours}} hours; customer support can also apply a change on behalf of either side. Every accepted change is re-priced: the guest pays a difference or is refunded part of what they paid, and the host's payout moves with it. Guests pay in their own currency and hosts are paid in theirs, across {{currencies}} currencies. Support, finance and the host performance team all need to know what was booked, what was changed, by whom, and what each change cost.
sections.problem: Design the data model. Cover: the reservation and how its terms (listing, dates, guest count, price breakdown) are versioned; the alteration request with its lifecycle (proposed, accepted, declined, expired, withdrawn) and who proposed and who responded; the price quote for the proposed terms and the difference against the terms in force; the guest charge or refund and the host payout adjustment that an accepted change creates, and how they stay linked to it; how the calendar is updated when new dates are accepted; and the facts that answer "nights and booking value by stay date after alterations", "alterations by who proposed them and how they ended" and "net revenue change caused by alterations per month".
sections.constraints: A reservation's terms at any past time must be reconstructable, including what both parties saw when they agreed. Money is stored as integers in minor units with its currency; amounts in different currencies are never added without a stated conversion. An accepted alteration and its money movements are either all recorded or none. Booking counts must not grow when a reservation is altered.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, shares, the response window and currency counts are hypothetical. Fee schedules are out of scope: a price quote is an input with line items (nightly total, cleaning fee, service fee, taxes). The reservation id never changes when the reservation is altered.
sections.criteria: Reservation identity separated from immutable terms versions; alteration requests with a full lifecycle and actors; a quote per proposed version and an explicit difference; money movements as records linked to the alteration, atomic with acceptance; calendar updated only on acceptance with an availability re-check; currency handling stated; facts that keep booking counts stable and attribute value by stay date; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: Can there be two open alteration requests on one reservation?
clarifications.a: No. In this exercise one request is open at a time; a new one replaces the old, which becomes withdrawn.

clarifications.q: Does a pending request hold the new nights on the calendar?
clarifications.a: No. Acceptance re-checks availability and fails if the new nights were booked in the meantime.

clarifications.q: Which exchange rate applies to a price difference?
clarifications.a: Your choice; state it. Many designs keep the rate locked at booking for the original amount and use the rate at acceptance for the difference.

clarifications.q: Can an alteration happen during the stay?
clarifications.a: Yes, to shorten or extend it; nights already stayed cannot be removed.

clarifications.q: Does support's change need the other side's acceptance?
clarifications.a: No, but it records the support agent and the reason, and both parties are notified.

hints: Separate the reservation's identity (one row, stable id) from its terms (immutable versions). An accepted alteration creates a new terms version; it never overwrites the old one.
The alteration request points to the version it would replace and to a proposed version with its own price quote. Acceptance is the moment the proposed version becomes current.
Money moves for an alteration are their own records (charge, refund, payout adjustment) keyed by the alteration, not edits to the original payment.
followups: A guest shortens a 7-night stay to 4 nights after check-in. Walk through the rows written: versions, request, quote, refund and payout adjustment.
The host accepts a date change, but the new nights were booked by another guest a minute earlier. Where does your model stop that, and what is recorded?
Finance wants booking value by stay date. A reservation was moved from March to May after March was reported. What changes in each month, and how is it labelled?
The guest pays in one currency and the host is paid in another. Show the difference for a one-night extension, with the rates you chose and where they are stored.
At {{daily_bookings}} bookings a day, which tables are OLTP and which are facts? How do you keep "reservations as of any date" cheap to query?

rules.ask: The guest disputes a charge and says they agreed to 5 nights, not 6. With the reservation row overwritten, how do you show what they agreed to and when?
If an alteration is a cancellation plus a new booking, what happens to booking counts, cancellation rates and the host's performance numbers?
The rate moved between booking and alteration. Which rate applies to the original amount and which to the difference, and where is each recorded?
An alteration lowers the price but a non-refundable part was already paid. How do you represent the part that is not refunded?
Which timestamp starts a new version: when the request was made, or when it was accepted? What does each choice do to "terms as of yesterday"?

incidents: With {{alteration_share}} of reservations altered, a backfill counted each accepted alteration as a new booking. Bookings for the quarter rose by about that share and the host performance team flagged hosts whose guests change plans often as having many cancellations.

A guest's request was accepted after {{response_hours}} hours had passed: the expiry job ran late, and the acceptance path did not check expiry. The reservation shows new dates that the guest believed had lapsed, and the guest was charged the difference.
A payment provider timeout left an accepted alteration with new dates on the calendar and no charge for the difference; a retry later charged it twice.

templates.title: Experiences — templates, scheduled instances, group capacity and private bookings
templates.subtopic: versioned templates, scheduled instances, capacity invariants, local time

sections.scenario: Besides stays, the marketplace sells experiences: a cooking class, a guided walk, a boat trip. There are about {{experiences}} active experiences. A host creates an experience (title, description, duration, what is included, a price per guest and a maximum group size of up to {{max_group}} here) and schedules instances of it at local times in the experience's city, some as one-offs and some from a weekly pattern. Guests book seats on an instance for themselves and companions. A guest can also book an instance privately for their own group at a group price; about {{private_share}} of booked instances are private. In this exercise's rules, an instance that has not reached the host's minimum number of guests {{min_guests_hours}} hours before the start may be cancelled by the host without penalty. Hosts can co-host with others, edit the experience over time and cancel single instances.
sections.problem: Design the data model. Cover: the experience and its versions (which fields may change after guests have booked, and what a booked guest is held to); co-hosts and their roles; schedules and instances, including how a weekly pattern turns into instances and how an edited pattern affects instances already booked; bookings and attendees with the price each guest agreed to; the capacity invariant for shared and private bookings and how it is enforced when two guests book the last seats at once; instance and booking cancellations with who cancelled and why; and the facts that answer "fill rate per instance and per host", "revenue per experience per month in the host's currency" and "cancellations by reason, including minimum not met".
sections.constraints: Booked seats on an instance never exceed its capacity, and a private booking excludes all other bookings for that instance. A guest is held to the description, start time and price that were in force when they booked. Instance times are local to the experience's city and must survive daylight-saving changes. Money is stored in integer minor units with its currency.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, group sizes, shares and the minimum-guest window are hypothetical. A group price for a private booking is set per experience version. A guest's companions may not have accounts; one booking names the booker and a guest count.
sections.criteria: Experience identity, versions, schedules and instances kept apart; bookings tied to the instance and the version they were sold under; a capacity invariant enforced transactionally for shared and private bookings; local time with a time zone identifier; cancellations with actor and reason, including minimum not met; fill rate and revenue defined at stated grains; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: Can a host lower the maximum group size after people have booked?
clarifications.a: Yes, but only for instances that are not already above the new size; existing bookings are honoured.

clarifications.q: Can a private booking be made on an instance that already has shared bookings?
clarifications.a: No. An instance is either private (one booking) or shared.

clarifications.q: What happens to booked guests when the host edits the description?
clarifications.a: Minor edits apply; changes to time, duration, meeting point or price do not apply to existing bookings without the guest's consent.

clarifications.q: Are instance times stored in UTC?
clarifications.a: Your choice. State how a 10:00 walk stays at 10:00 local time after the clocks change.

clarifications.q: Who counts as the host for reporting?
clarifications.a: The primary host; co-hosts are tracked separately with their role.

hints: Separate the experience (identity), its versions (content and price), the schedule (a rule) and instances (concrete dated occurrences). Bookings reference an instance and the version they were sold under.

Capacity is an invariant on the instance: keep a seats-taken counter updated in the same transaction as the booking, with a check, or lock the instance row; compare it with a sum over bookings in a reconciliation.
Store the instance's local date and time with the city's time zone identifier, and derive the UTC instant from them.
followups: Two guests try to book the last 3 seats of an instance at the same moment, one shared and one private. What happens, and which rows are written?
A weekly pattern is moved from Saturday to Sunday. What happens to future Saturday instances that already have bookings, and to those without?
The host raises the price. Which guests pay the new price, and how does revenue reporting know?
Define fill rate precisely: seats or instances, which instances are in the denominator (cancelled, private, minimum not met), and when an instance's number is final.
At {{experiences}} experiences with weekly patterns, how far ahead do you create instance rows, and what is computed on demand?

rules.ask: Two bookings commit at the same moment for the last seats. Show the statement or lock that keeps the counter from going negative.
The clocks go back an hour in the experience's city. Does next Saturday's 10:00 walk still start at 10:00 local time in your model?
A private booking is cancelled two days before the instance. Does the instance reopen for shared bookings, and what does your fill rate say about it?
Do you store every future instance or only the pattern? What happens to a booked instance when the pattern changes?
Is a private booking of 2 guests on an instance for {{max_group}} a full instance or a 2-seat one in your metric?

incidents: A host lowered the maximum group size to below {{max_group}} while instances were already partly booked. A job that recomputed capacity from the experience's current version marked those instances as over capacity and cancelled the latest bookings automatically.
After a daylight-saving change, instances generated from weekly patterns in one region started an hour early for two weeks: the pattern had been expanded with a fixed UTC offset.

About {{private_share}} of booked instances are private, and fill-rate dashboards counted each private booking's guest count against the shared group size, so hosts with many private bookings appeared to run nearly empty instances.

templates.title: Two-sided reviews — hidden until both submit, then published, answered and sometimes removed
templates.subtopic: visibility rules as data, review lifecycle, sub-ratings, aggregate ratings with removals

sections.scenario: After about {{daily_checkouts}} checkouts a day, the guest can review the stay and the host can review the guest. In this exercise's rules, each review stays hidden from the other party until both have submitted or the review window of {{review_window_days}} days after checkout closes, whichever comes first; then both are published together, or the one that exists is published alone. A guest's review has an overall rating and sub-ratings (cleanliness, accuracy, check-in, communication, location, value) plus optional private feedback that only the host sees. The host may post one public response to a published review. Reviews that break the content policy are removed after a report; about {{removal_share}} of reviews are removed this way. A listing shows its average rating only after it has {{min_reviews_shown}} published reviews.
sections.problem: Design the data model. Cover: the review per reservation and author role, with its states (eligible, draft, submitted, published, removed) and the timestamps that drive them; how "hidden until both submit or the window closes" is represented so that no read path can leak a hidden review; sub-ratings and how new categories added later are handled; private feedback and who may read it; responses; reports and removals, with reason and appeal; and the derived listing rating (overall and per sub-rating) with how it changes when a review is published or removed. Include the facts that answer "review rate after checkout, by role", "average rating per listing over time" and "reviews removed by policy reason".
sections.constraints: A hidden review is never visible to the other party, in the product or in any data the other party can query. A published review's text and ratings never change; removal hides it from guests and hosts but keeps it for audit. The listing rating must be reproducible for any past date. Private feedback never appears in public data or in aggregates shown to anyone but the host.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, the window, the display threshold and the removal share are hypothetical. Review text is moderated by a separate service that returns a decision; only the decision and reason are modelled here. Times are stored as instants; the window is measured from checkout in the listing's time zone.
sections.criteria: One review per reservation and role with states and timestamps; publication derived from "both submitted or window closed" and enforced in one place; long-form sub-ratings with the categories asked; private feedback isolated with access rules; responses versioned; removals as states with reason and appeal, never deletes; listing rating as a dated derived series with a threshold and a stated restatement rule; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: Can a review be edited after submitting?
clarifications.a: Not in this exercise. A draft can be edited until it is submitted.

clarifications.q: Does a removed review still count in the listing's rating?
clarifications.a: No. It is removed from the rating from the time of removal; whether past ratings are restated is your decision, stated.

clarifications.q: Can a host's response be edited?
clarifications.a: Yes, within a short period after posting; keep the versions.

clarifications.q: When exactly does the window close?
clarifications.a: At the end of the last day of the window, in the listing's local time, counted from the checkout date.

clarifications.q: Can the guest see that the host has already reviewed them?
clarifications.a: Yes, that it exists; never what it says or the rating.

hints: Store the review once with submitted_at and a computed published_at (the earlier of "both submitted" and window close); visibility is a rule on published_at, applied in one place.
Keep sub-ratings in long form (review, category, score) so a new category does not change the table, and record which categories were asked on that review.
Treat the listing rating as a derived, dated series built from publication and removal events, not a counter updated in place.
followups: The host submits on day 2, the guest never does. When and how is the host's review published, and which job or query makes it happen?
A new sub-rating category is added. How do averages treat older reviews that never had it?
A review is removed 40 days after publication. What happens to the listing rating for last month's report, and to the host's performance numbers?
Analysts query reviews in the warehouse. How do you stop a hidden review or private feedback from reaching a dashboard the other party can see?
Write the definition of the listing rating shown on a date, with the display threshold of {{min_reviews_shown}} reviews and removals.

rules.ask: A job sets the flag when both have submitted. The job fails for a day. What does the guest see, and what would derive visibility from timestamps instead?
A review is removed. Do you recompute the average from published reviews, or subtract from a stored sum? What does each do for a past date?
A new category is added next quarter. What happens to the table, to old rows and to the averages?
Which tables hold private feedback, who can query them, and how do you prove it never reaches a public aggregate?
Removal is for policy reasons and may be appealed. What do you delete, what do you keep, and what can an appeal restore?

incidents: A pipeline computed window close in UTC instead of the listing's local time. For listings far from UTC, some reviews were published a few hours before the {{review_window_days}}-day window had closed, while the other party was still writing.

After a large batch of removals, listing pages kept showing the old averages for days: the rating was a cached sum that only ever increased, so removed reviews (normally about {{removal_share}} of all reviews) were never taken out of it.

A host-facing dashboard computed a weekly average from submitted reviews instead of published ones. For listings below {{min_reviews_shown}} published reviews, where no rating should be shown at all, a host could read a guest's still-hidden rating from the change in the weekly number.

templates.title: Pricing settings — base, custom dates, weekend and length-of-stay discounts, and the price actually offered
templates.subtopic: effective-dated rules, bitemporal settings, quotes as evidence

sections.scenario: Each of about {{listings}} listings has pricing settings that the host changes often (about {{setting_changes}} changes a day across all listings): a base nightly price, an optional different weekend price, custom prices for chosen dates, a cleaning fee, and length-of-stay discounts, for example {{weekly_discount}} off stays of 7 nights or more and a larger discount for 28 nights or more. In this exercise's rules only the largest length-of-stay discount that applies is used, and "weekend" means Friday and Saturday nights in the listing's local time. Search results and listing pages show quotes for dates the guest chose, about {{quotes_per_day}} quotes a day, and the booking charges the quote the guest accepted. Support regularly hears "the price changed between search and checkout", and the pricing team wants to know which settings were in force when a price was offered.
sections.problem: Design the data model. Cover: how settings are stored so that the price of any night can be computed for any past moment (when a setting was in force and for which nights it applies are different times); custom date prices and their precedence over weekend and base prices; length-of-stay discounts and the rule that only one applies; the quote as a record of what was offered (inputs, settings version, line items, currency, expiry); how a booking links to the quote it charged; a materialised nightly price calendar and how it stays consistent with the settings; and the facts that answer "average nightly price offered per market and stay date", "share of bookings that used a length-of-stay discount" and "searches whose quoted total differed from the checkout total, and why".
sections.constraints: For any listing, night and past instant, the price that would have been quoted must be reproducible. A booking's charge equals a stored quote. Settings are never edited in place; a change is a new record. Money is in integer minor units in the listing's currency, and a currency change is itself a dated setting.
sections.assumptions: Listing counts, change and quote volumes, and discount sizes are hypothetical. Taxes and service fees are added after the nightly total and are out of scope except as quote line items. Price suggestions, if a host uses them, arrive as setting changes like any other.
sections.criteria: Settings as typed, effective-dated, append-only rules with system time and valid nights kept apart; explicit precedence and a single-discount rule; quotes stored as evidence with the settings version and line items, and bookings that reference them; a materialised calendar tagged with its version and reconciled; retention for quotes stated; local-date weekend logic; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: Which wins when a night has a custom price and is also a weekend night?
clarifications.a: The custom price. Precedence is custom date price, then weekend price, then base price.

clarifications.q: Is the length-of-stay discount applied per night or to the total?
clarifications.a: To the nightly total of the stay, before the cleaning fee, in this exercise.

clarifications.q: Do we keep every quote shown in search?
clarifications.a: Your choice. Say what you keep, for how long, and how you answer a support case about a quote you did not keep.

clarifications.q: Can a host change settings for nights already booked?
clarifications.a: Yes, but it never changes an existing booking's price.

clarifications.q: Does a quote expire?
clarifications.a: Yes; your choice of how long, stated. Checkout re-quotes after expiry.

hints: There are two times: when a setting was in force (system time) and which nights it applies to (valid nights). Store both explicitly, so "the price of 12 March as seen on 1 February" is a lookup, not a guess.
Keep base, weekend, custom date and discount settings as typed, effective-dated rules; compute a nightly calendar from them for serving, tagged with the settings version it came from.
A quote is evidence: store its inputs, the settings version, line items and expiry, and let the booking reference it by id.
followups: Compute the total for a 7-night stay from Thursday that includes one custom-priced night, with the {{weekly_discount}} weekly discount. Which rows did you read?
The host changed the weekend price at 14:00; a guest searched at 13:59 and booked at 14:05. What did they see, what were they charged, and how does your model show both?
At {{quotes_per_day}} quotes a day, which quotes do you keep in full, which as aggregates, and for how long?
A market analyst wants the average nightly price for New Year's Eve as it evolved over the three months before. Which table answers that, and at what cost?
The listing's currency changes. What happens to custom date prices already set, to the calendar, and to open quotes?

rules.ask: The host changes the base price. How do you answer "what would this night have cost if booked yesterday"?
Which of your two times does the search cache key on, and which does a support agent need?
A listing is twelve hours ahead of UTC. From which value do you compute the weekday of a night, and what goes wrong if it is a UTC timestamp?
Both the weekly and the monthly discount apply to a 30-night stay. Show where your model enforces that only the larger one is used.
A setting changes. How quickly does the calendar reflect it, and what does a quote served from the stale calendar say about which version it used?

incidents: A release applied the weekly and the monthly discount together for 28-night stays. For a day, long stays were quoted and booked below the host's settings; with discounts like {{weekly_discount}} stacking, some hosts' payouts fell sharply.

The nightly calendar fell behind the settings by up to an hour during a pre-holiday burst of setting changes, several times the usual {{setting_changes}} a day. Guests saw one total in search and another at checkout, and support could not tell which version each had seen.
Weekend prices were applied to Saturday and Sunday nights for listings east of UTC: the weekday was computed from a UTC timestamp instead of the night's local date.

templates.title: Double-booked nights from confirmed reservations and their alterations
templates.subtopic: half-open date ranges, effective state from alterations, per-night coverage

sections.scenario: A stays marketplace takes bookings for listings in {{city_list}}. A reservation covers the nights from check_in (inclusive) to check_out (exclusive): a guest who checks out on the 5th and a guest who checks in on the 5th share no night. Guests and hosts change bookings through alterations, which the other party accepts or declines; {{alter_rule}} Calendars are synchronised with channel managers and imported calendars, and sometimes two bookings land on the same night anyway. Operations wants the listings where that happened and the size of each problem, so hosts can be contacted before guests arrive.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns listing_id, city, overbooked_nights, excess_stay_nights, reservations_involved, first_night, one row per listing that has at least one overbooked night, ordered by excess_stay_nights descending, then listing_id. Only reservations whose status is 'confirmed' count. A reservation's stay is the new_check_in and new_check_out of its accepted alteration with the latest resolved_at; if it has no accepted alteration, its stay is its own check_in and check_out. Declined and pending alterations change nothing. A night is overbooked when more counted stays cover it than the listing has units. {{units_rule}} overbooked_nights is the number of distinct overbooked nights; excess_stay_nights is the sum, over those nights, of the stays covering the night minus units; reservations_involved is the number of distinct reservations covering at least one overbooked night; first_night is the earliest overbooked night.
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). Stays are half-open date ranges. The sample has {{listings_n}} listings, {{reservations_n}} reservations and {{alterations_n}} alterations; production has hundreds of millions of reservations, many of them long stays.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical schema, listings, guests and dates. check_in and check_out on reservations are the dates as first booked and are not updated by alterations. A listing's units does not change during the period shown.
