sections.criteria: Confirmed reservations only; effective stay from the latest accepted alteration with the original dates as fallback; half-open night coverage; overbooked nights against the listing's units; distinct nights, excess and distinct reservations exactly as defined; deterministic ordering; can explain the sweep alternative, an exclusion constraint and its limits, and how to choose which stay to relocate.

clarifications.q: Does a stay checking out on the day another checks in overlap it?
clarifications.a: No. The check-out date is not a night of the stay.

clarifications.q: Do pending requests or cancelled bookings hold nights?
clarifications.a: No. Only status 'confirmed' counts.

clarifications.q: A reservation was altered twice and both were accepted. Which dates apply?
clarifications.a: The accepted alteration with the latest resolved_at.

clarifications.q: Should listings with no overbooked night appear with zeros?
clarifications.a: No. Only listings with at least one overbooked night.

clarifications.q: Two confirmed reservations have identical dates. Is that one booking?
clarifications.a: No. They are two reservations and both count; it is the worst kind of double booking.

hints: First build one row per counted reservation with its effective stay: pick the latest accepted alteration per reservation (DISTINCT ON or ROW_NUMBER) and COALESCE it over the original dates.
Expand each stay into its nights (generate_series over 0 .. check_out - check_in - 1 added to check_in), then count stays per listing and night.
Keep the overbooked (listing, night) rows, aggregate them per listing, and join back to the nights to count the reservations involved.
followups: Rewrite it without expanding stays into nights: a sweep with +1 at check-in and −1 at check-out (a running sum over a window), then gaps-and-islands for the overbooked ranges.
How would PostgreSQL itself have refused the second booking? Describe an exclusion constraint on daterange(check_in, check_out), and why it does not work as written for listings with units above 1.
For each overbooked night, which reservation should be relocated? Write the query that ranks the stays on a night by booked_at and returns those beyond units.
Production has long monthly stays. How many rows does the night expansion produce per year, and how would you partition and run this daily?

rules.ask: Does BETWEEN check_in AND check_out include the check-out date? What does your query say about a guest leaving on the morning another arrives?
A night is covered by three stays. How many pairs does your self join produce, and what does that do to the night count?
Expanding is fine on the sample. A 120-night stay expands into 120 rows; what does that cost at production scale, and what would you do instead?
Is the latest alteration the latest accepted one? Which timestamp decides, and what happens to a pending request made after an accepted one?
A listing has 2 units and 3 stays on one night. Which stays are "involved", and how many guests need to be moved?

incidents: A dashboard built with BETWEEN check_in AND check_out counted every same-day turnover as a double booking, and hosts with back-to-back stays were sent warnings; this report, with half-open stays, showed none for them.

A host lowered a listing's units from 2 to 1 after taking a room off the market. Future nights already holding two confirmed stays became overbooked at once, and nobody was told until this report ran.

During a slow-network spell a guest pressed Book twice and two confirmed reservations with identical dates were created a second apart. They appear here on the same nights; support wants to know which one to cancel.

templates.title: Search by date range: availability, total stay price, map area and guests
templates.subtopic: availability index, stay pricing, freshness from calendar changes

sections.scenario: Guests search a marketplace of {{listings}} active listings by drawing or moving a map area (or typing a place that resolves to one), choosing check-in and check-out dates and a number of guests, and narrowing by price range, property type and amenities. A result is useful only if the listing can actually be booked for that whole stay: every night free, check-in allowed on that day, the stay within the listing's minimum and maximum nights, inside its advance-notice and how-far-ahead windows, and room for the guests. Each result shows the total price of the stay, built from that listing's nightly prices (a base price, a weekend price, custom prices on particular dates), a length-of-stay discount and a cleaning fee. Searches peak at {{qps}} per second. Calendars and prices change all the time: bookings, cancellations, hosts blocking nights, prices edited by hosts, and calendars synced from channel managers and imported calendar feeds, about {{calendar_updates}} changes per second at peak.
sections.problem: Design the search serving system. Cover the index (how listings are partitioned, and how a year of nightly availability and prices is stored per listing), how a query is answered (map area, guests and filters, then the date-range check, then the total price, then hand-off to ranking), the update path from a calendar or price change to the index within {{staleness}}, how search and booking stay honest with each other, and how map pins and result pages stay stable while the guest pans, zooms and pages.
sections.constraints: First-page search latency p99 under 400 ms, including ranking. A change to a listing's calendar or prices must be reflected in search within {{staleness}} at p99. Search may be slightly stale, but booking must check availability and price exactly against the listing's calendar. Stays of 1 to 90 nights, up to a year ahead. A listing's calendar dates are its own local dates.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, latencies and rules are hypothetical; the price rules (weekend price, custom per-date prices, a weekly discount from 7 nights and a monthly one from 28, a cleaning fee per stay) are this exercise's rules. A calendar service is the source of truth for each listing's nights and settings and emits a change event with a per-listing version for every change. A ranking model exists and takes up to a few thousand candidates with features; you design what reaches it, not the model. Taxes are added at checkout.
sections.criteria: Separates the slowly changing filter attributes from per-listing nightly availability and prices held in compact arrays; a constant-time stay check (free-run lengths or bit masks) plus the separate check-in, length, notice and window rules; totals from prefix sums and the stated discount and fee rules; geo partitioning that copes with dense and sparse areas, with a candidate budget handed to ranking; an update path from versioned calendar events that is idempotent, coalesces per listing, isolates bulk syncs and is measured against {{staleness}}; booking as the exact check, with price differences explained to the guest; stable paging through a result snapshot; listing-local dates handled without time-zone conversion; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Can search ever show a listing that is no longer available?
clarifications.a: Only within {{staleness}} of the change. After that it is a bug. Booking re-checks either way.

clarifications.q: Are flexible dates in scope ("a weekend in March")?
clarifications.a: Not for the first design; it is a follow-up.

clarifications.q: In which currency is the total shown?
clarifications.a: The guest's. Exchange rates refresh daily; checkout recomputes in the listing's currency.

clarifications.q: How many results does a query return?
clarifications.a: A first page of 20 to 50 ranked listings, plus pins for up to a few hundred in the visible map area.

clarifications.q: Does the price filter apply to the nightly price or the total?
clarifications.a: Your choice; say which and why. Guests read it as "what will this stay cost me".

hints: Split the query into the cheap, slowly changing part (area, guests, property type, amenities) and the expensive, fast-changing part (nights and prices for the chosen dates). Keep the second in a compact per-listing structure you can check in constant time.

A year of nights fits in a few hundred bits per listing. A stay from day d for n nights is free if bits d to d+n−1 are all set; precomputing, for every day, the length of the free run that starts there makes that one lookup. The rules on check-in day, minimum nights and advance notice are separate checks.
A prefix sum over the nightly price array gives any stay's subtotal in one subtraction; the discount and fee are applied afterwards.
followups: Walk me through one query for 3 guests and 5 nights over a dense city centre: which partitions are touched, what is filtered where, and how many candidates reach ranking?
A guest books a listing. Trace the change to the index, and say what keeps the update within {{staleness}} and what happens when the update path falls behind.
A guest sees one total in search and a higher one at checkout. Where can the two diverge, and how do you bound or explain the difference?
Add flexible dates ("any 3 nights in the next 6 weeks"). What changes in the index and the query cost?
The guest pans the map and goes to page 3 while availability changes underneath. How do you keep pages without duplicates or gaps, and what do the pins show?

rules.ask: How do you store a year of nightly availability and prices per listing in that index, and what does one calendar change cost to apply at {{calendar_updates}} changes per second?
One viewport over a dense city centre holds tens of thousands of listings and another over open countryside holds a dozen. How does your partitioning keep both fast and evenly loaded?
What is the cache key when every guest picks different dates, guests and filters? What hit rate do you expect, and what happens to cached results when a calendar changes?
Show me the exact check for a 5-night stay starting on a day the listing does not allow check-in, 2 days from now with 3 days' advance notice. Which checks are not about the night bits at all?
How many listing-nights does one query over a city touch if availability is rows in a table, and can that meet 400 ms at {{qps}} searches per second?

incidents: During a holiday booking rush the index update path falls 40 minutes behind. Guests click listings that search shows as free, find the dates taken at booking, and failed booking attempts triple.

A channel manager re-syncs the full calendars of 80,000 listings at once on top of the normal {{calendar_updates}} changes per second; ordinary hosts' bookings and blocks queue behind it and stop meeting the target of {{staleness}}.

A change to the indexer converts each listing's local calendar dates through UTC timestamps. For listings east of UTC, every night shifts by one day: guests are shown free nights that are booked and miss nights that are free.
After a currency-rate refresh fails, totals for guests paying in one currency are computed with a week-old rate, and the price filter drops listings that are inside the guest's range.

templates.title: Demand signals for price suggestions: searches, views, booking pace and comparable listings
templates.subtopic: demand by market and stay night, comparables, measuring suggestions

sections.scenario: Hosts set their own nightly prices. The marketplace offers each host optional price suggestions for every future night up to {{horizon_days}} days ahead, refreshed {{refresh}}; a host can accept them, ignore them, or turn on automatic pricing within a minimum and maximum they choose. The suggestions are only as good as the signals behind them: search demand for each of {{markets}} markets and each future stay night (from about {{searches_per_day}} searches a day, many with dates), listing views and wishlist saves, booking pace (how much of a night's capacity is already booked at each lead time, against the same lead time a year earlier), remaining supply, and comparable listings with their prices and booking outcomes. The team is also asked to show whether suggestions help hosts and guests.
sections.problem: Design the signal platform. Cover how raw search, view and booking events become demand per market × stay night × lead time; how repeated searches and automated traffic are kept from inflating demand; how comparable listings are chosen and summarised; how signals are kept point-in-time correct for training and served to the suggestion model {{refresh}}; how acceptance and outcomes are fed back; and how you would measure whether suggestions help, given that hosts in one market compete for the same guests.
sections.constraints: Suggestions are advice; the host's price is final. Training data must use only what was known when a suggestion was made. A host must never be able to see a particular competitor's prices or bookings through the comparables: only aggregates over at least 10 listings are shown. Search events carry a pseudonymous visitor id, not a person's identity, and are kept for 13 months in raw form.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, windows and thresholds are hypothetical. Search, listing-view, wishlist and booking events arrive on a durable event stream; each search with dates names a market (or a map area that maps to one or more markets), a check-in date, a check-out date and a guest count. Listing calendars and prices are available as daily snapshots and as change events.
sections.criteria: Clear demand definitions per stay night and check-in date with deduplication by visitor; bot filtering whose error is measured; booking pace against a seasonal baseline; comparables chosen on attributes and location with k-anonymous aggregates (at least 10 listings); point-in-time correct signal tables (as known on day T) for training and serving; feedback of acceptance and outcomes with the suggestion logged; a measurement design that handles interference (market-level or time-based randomisation) and selection bias in observational comparisons; guards against feedback loops; freshness matched to need; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Is one search for 5 nights 5 units of demand?
clarifications.a: Your call. Define demand per stay night and per check-in date, and say which question each answers.

clarifications.q: Can we tell whether a search led to a booking?
clarifications.a: Searches, views and bookings share the pseudonymous visitor id within a session; attribution beyond that is up to you.

clarifications.q: How much of the search traffic is automated?
clarifications.a: A meaningful share. Each session has a bot score that is useful but imperfect.

clarifications.q: Can we test suggestions host by host?
clarifications.a: You can randomise however you like; tell me what competition between nearby hosts does to the result.

clarifications.q: Do hosts in a market all see the same suggestion?
clarifications.a: No; each listing gets its own, but they share the market's demand signal.

hints: Deduplicate before counting: one visitor searching the same market and nights twenty times in a day is one unit of interest. Expand a date range into its nights, and count per (market, night, day observed).
Booking pace needs a baseline: booked share of capacity at lead time L this year against the same lead time last year, aligned by weekday and around holidays.

When treated and control hosts compete for the same guests, a host-level test measures a transfer, not a gain. Randomise by market, or alternate treatment over time, and accept the cost in statistical power.
followups: Define "demand for market M on night D as known on day T". Show the table, its grain, and how a late or duplicate event changes it.
How do you build comparable listings, and how do you keep any host from inferring one competitor's prices or bookings from the aggregates?
A large event is announced for one city five months ahead. How quickly do your signals react, and what stops a short spike from moving prices for months?
How do you measure whether suggestions raise host earnings and bookings, given competition between hosts and markets of very different sizes?
Suggestions change prices, prices change booking pace, and booking pace feeds the next suggestion. How do you keep the model from learning its own suggestions back?

rules.ask: Treated hosts accept lower suggestions and take bookings from control hosts nearby. What does your listing-level test measure then, and how would you randomise instead?
Your bot filter removes sessions above a score threshold. How do you know what share of real guests it removes, and what happens to demand when a scraper learns to look human?
Which of your signals actually needs to be fresher than {{refresh}}, and what does running it in real time cost you?
Show me how a training row for a suggestion made 60 days before the night gets the demand and booking pace values exactly as known that day.
Booked prices exist only for listings that sold. What bias does that put in your comparable-price signal, and how do you correct for it?

incidents: A scraper starts searching every date range in one city every few minutes. Demand for that city triples overnight and suggestions for 3,000 listings rise by 20% before anyone notices.

The booking feed into the signal pipeline stalls for two days with no alarm. Booking pace in all {{markets}} markets reads as a collapse, and suggestions fall by up to 30% for hosts who use automatic pricing.
A search-page change starts sending next weekend's dates by default when a guest browses the map without choosing dates. Demand for next-weekend nights jumps in every market at once.
Suggestions are refreshed {{refresh}}, but a dashboard shows that hosts who accepted them earned less than hosts who did not; product asks whether to switch suggestions off.

templates.title: Fraud labels that arrive late and disagree: training sets and loss reporting
templates.subtopic: label ledger, label maturity, point-in-time training sets, restatements

sections.scenario: A stays marketplace takes about {{bookings_per_day}} bookings a day. Risk models score bookings, accounts and listings for fraud: payments with stolen cards, taken-over accounts, fake listings, and requests to pay outside the platform. The models are retrained {{cadence}}, and leadership reads a monthly fraud-loss report. The labels both depend on come from {{sources}} sources that arrive late and disagree: card chargebacks up to {{dispute_window}} days after payment (this exercise's dispute window; check current card-network rules), each with a reason code; reports from guests and hosts; trust-team review decisions, some later reversed on appeal; refunds granted because a listing did not exist; and account-security events. One booking can collect several labels that conflict, and a label on an account may or may not apply to each of its bookings.
sections.problem: Design the label platform. Cover how every label is recorded (source, entity, what it asserts, when it happened, when we learned it, and what superseded it); how conflicting labels are resolved into one outcome per entity, and how that rule is versioned; when a label is mature enough to train on or report; how training sets are built point-in-time correct and reproducibly; what you do about bookings the model blocked, which never get an outcome; how monthly loss reports are restated when late labels arrive; and which data-quality checks catch a source that silently changes.
sections.constraints: A training set must be rebuildable exactly, months later. A month's loss report, once published, changes only through a recorded restatement. Reviewers' free-text notes and messages never enter training sets; only coded outcomes do. A label on one account must not mark unrelated bookings, such as the bookings of a guest whose account was taken over, as fraud by that guest.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, windows and rates are hypothetical. Bookings, payments, refunds, chargebacks, reports and review decisions are available as event streams or daily extracts, each with its own event time. Model features are already stored point-in-time correct; this design is about labels.
sections.criteria: An append-only label ledger with event time and knowledge time, source and supersession; a versioned, owned resolution rule per entity; label maturity tied to the {{dispute_window}}-day window, with immature bookings excluded or weighted rather than treated as clean; point-in-time, reproducible training sets built from ledger snapshots; a plan for blocked traffic (random allow-through or reviewed sample with logged probabilities); account labels propagated to bookings with care for victims; restatements recorded and explained, with as-published and as-restated views; source-level quality checks (code distributions, volume, lag) that alert; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Which source wins when two disagree?
clarifications.a: There is no agreed rule today; propose one, and say who owns it.

clarifications.q: Does every chargeback mean fraud?
clarifications.a: No. Reason codes separate fraud from "service not received" and other disputes, and a merchant can win a dispute later.

clarifications.q: How long until we know a booking was clean?
clarifications.a: Never with certainty. Most fraud chargebacks arrive within weeks; a few take nearly the whole {{dispute_window}}-day window.

clarifications.q: Do blocked bookings get labels?
clarifications.a: No outcome is ever observed for a booking that was blocked.

clarifications.q: Who reads the loss report?
clarifications.a: Finance and leadership, monthly, with quarter-end numbers used externally.

hints: Keep labels as an append-only ledger with two times per label: when the event happened and when you learned of it. "What we knew on date T" is then a filter, not a reconstruction.
A booking younger than its label window is not "clean"; it is not yet known. Train and evaluate only on mature bookings, or weight immature ones by how much of their outcome has usually arrived.
To learn anything about blocked traffic you need a small, random, logged allow-through (or a review queue) with known probabilities.
followups: Show the label ledger's schema and the resolution query that turns it into one outcome per booking as known on a date.
The model retrained {{cadence}} looks better on recent bookings than on older ones. What is going on, and how do you evaluate it honestly?
How do you estimate the true fraud rate among bookings the model blocked?
A trust-team decision is reversed on appeal two months later. What changes in the ledger, the training sets already built, and the published reports?
How do you detect, within a day, that one of the {{sources}} label sources has silently changed what it sends?

rules.ask: If labels are updated in place, how do you rebuild last quarter's training set exactly as it was, and explain why the old model behaved as it did?
A chargeback for fraud arrives on day 110 for a booking already in a published report and in two training sets. Walk me through what changes where.
Bookings from the last two weeks have no chargebacks yet. If you label them clean, what does that do to the model and to its measured precision?
An account is confirmed as taken over. Which of its bookings get a fraud label, and which are victims' bookings?
The model blocks 2% of bookings and you never see their outcome. How does that bias the next model, and what does it cost to correct?

incidents: The payment processor changes its chargeback reason codes; one code that meant fraud is split in two, and for three weeks fraud chargebacks are mapped to "other". The month's reported fraud loss drops by a third and nobody questions it.

A trust-team bulk action against a fraud ring labels 12,000 accounts; 2,000 of those labels are reversed on appeal a month later, after one of the retrains, run {{cadence}}, has already learned from them.
The retrain uses bookings up to yesterday and treats those without labels as clean. Measured precision on recent bookings rises at each retrain while actual fraud losses climb.

Guest reports arrive as free text and an extraction step turns them into coded labels. After a change to it, negated phrases such as "definitely not a scam" are read as fake-listing reports, and fake-listing labels double in one week.

templates.title: Guest–host messaging: ordered delivery, translation, response metrics and safety scanning
templates.subtopic: per-thread ordering, delivery receipts, translation, safety holds, metrics

sections.scenario: Guests and hosts message each other before booking (inquiries), after booking, during the stay and after it. A thread can include co-hosts and a host's team members. About {{messages_per_day}} messages a day are delivered to mobile apps (with push notifications), to the web and by email, where a reply by email must land in the right thread. Messages can be automatically translated between {{languages}} languages, always with the original one tap away. Messages are scanned for safety: requests to pay outside the platform, phishing links and harassment. Hosts' response rate and response time (the share of inquiries and booking requests answered within {{response_window}}, and the time to the first reply) are shown on listings and feed host standards.
sections.problem: Design the messaging system. Cover how messages are stored and ordered within a thread, how they are delivered to every participant's devices with delivery and read receipts, how offline devices catch up, how email replies are matched to threads, where translation happens and how it is cached, how safety scanning works within a hold budget of {{hold_budget}} per message and what happens to a message found harmful after delivery, and how response-rate and response-time metrics are computed so that they are fair to hosts.
sections.constraints: Messages in a thread appear in the same order on every device. Sending must feel instant: the sender sees the message accepted within 200 ms. A message may be held for scanning for at most {{hold_budget}}; anything that needs longer is scanned after delivery. Translation must never block delivery. Before a booking is confirmed, phone numbers and email addresses in messages are masked (this exercise's rule). Messages are kept for the life of the reservation plus a retention period, and their text never enters analytics tables.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, budgets and rules are hypothetical. Push notifications go through the mobile platforms' public push services, which can delay or drop a notification. A translation service and a fast and a slow safety classifier exist; you decide how to call them.
sections.criteria: Per-thread ordering through a single writer and server-assigned sequence numbers (not device clocks); durable accept within 200 ms, then fan-out to devices with idempotent display and sync by sequence; receipts as separate events; email replies matched with signed reply addresses; translation on read with caching and the original always available; two-stage safety scanning within {{hold_budget}}, retraction after delivery with notices; contact masking before booking; response metrics on server receipt times, with personal replies only, fair exclusions for platform outages and a robust statistic; message text kept out of analytics; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Do automatic replies and scheduled messages count as responses?
clarifications.a: In this exercise, scheduled messages and automatic replies do not count as a response; a first personal reply does.

clarifications.q: Who counts as "the host" for response metrics?
clarifications.a: Any host, co-host or team member in the thread.

clarifications.q: Can a message be edited or unsent?
clarifications.a: No edits. A message can be removed by the safety team; the thread shows that a message was removed.

clarifications.q: How long may a thread be?
clarifications.a: Most have a few dozen messages; some long stays reach thousands.

clarifications.q: Are messages end-to-end encrypted?
clarifications.a: Not in this exercise; the platform reads them to scan and translate, under its terms.

hints: Give each thread a single writer for ordering (route by thread id) and assign a per-thread sequence number at accept time; devices sync "everything after sequence N".
Keep translation out of the send path: translate on first read into a language, cache by (message, target language), and show the original if translation is slow.
Two-stage scanning: a fast classifier inside the hold budget decides deliver, hold or mask; a slower one runs after delivery and can retract with a notice to the recipient.
followups: Walk through a guest's message from send to the host's phone, the co-host's laptop and an email inbox. Which steps are synchronous?
A host's phone was offline for two days. How does it catch up without missing or reordering messages, and what do read receipts say?
The slow classifier flags a message an hour after delivery as a phishing link. What do the recipient, the sender and the metrics see?
How do you compute response rate (answered within {{response_window}}) and response time so that a push-service outage or an inquiry sent at 3 a.m. local time is fair to the host?
Long-stay threads reach thousands of messages and many photos. What changes in storage and sync?

rules.ask: The push service drops a notification and the app's connection is closed. How does the host's device learn the message exists, and how quickly?
How do you keep per-thread order through that queue when one thread has a burst of 50 messages and partitions are rebalanced?
Two participants send at the same instant from devices whose clocks differ by 40 seconds. Which order does everyone see, and why is it the same everywhere?
A thread with {{languages}} possible languages and 3 participants: how many translations do you compute per message, when, and what does a translation error cost?
Response time averaged per host is dominated by one inquiry answered after a week. What statistic and window would you show, and why?

incidents: The translation service slows to 4 seconds per request. Because translation was put in the delivery path, senders see messages stuck on "sending" and some resend, creating duplicates.
A phishing campaign sends look-alike payment links to 50,000 guests. The fast classifier misses them; the slow one is updated six hours later, after most were delivered and opened.

A push-notification outage lasting three hours in one region delays hosts' awareness of inquiries; that quarter's response metrics for hosts in the region drop, though nothing changed in their behaviour.
The safety hold is raised from {{hold_budget}} to 10 seconds after an incident; inquiry-to-booking conversion falls noticeably and support contacts about "message not sent" rise.

templates.title: Quarterly host standards: assessment, progress, history and appeals
templates.subtopic: versioned definitions, as-of assessments, appeals and recomputation

sections.scenario: Every quarter the marketplace assesses about {{hosts}} hosts against this exercise's host standard: a response rate of at least 90%, a host cancellation rate under 1% (cancellations covered by an approved extenuating-circumstances decision do not count), an overall rating of at least 4.8, and at least {{min_stays}} completed stays, all measured over {{window}}. Hosts who meet it get a badge on their listings and a search benefit for the next quarter. During the quarter, hosts see their progress. After an assessment, a host may appeal within {{appeal_days}} days, for example because a cancellation should have been excused. The inputs come from bookings, alterations and cancellations, messages, two-sided reviews (hidden until both sides submit or the review window closes, so ratings arrive after the stay), and extenuating-circumstance decisions that can be approved weeks after the event.
sections.problem: Design the assessment platform. Cover how each metric is defined (with its version), which data cut-off an assessment uses, how the quarterly assessment is computed and published at the same moment for every host, how hosts' progress is shown during the quarter, how a host's status history and the inputs behind each assessment are kept, how an appeal or a late exception changes a past assessment without silently rewriting history, and how you would audit that the badge and the search benefit match the published assessment.
sections.constraints: An assessment must be reproducible from its recorded inputs and definition version. A host must be able to see why they did or did not meet the standard, down to the stays, cancellations and reviews counted. Results publish within 3 days of the quarter's end, at one time for all hosts. A change after an appeal takes effect immediately and is recorded as a new version of that assessment.
sections.assumptions: All counts, thresholds and timings are hypothetical, and the standard is this exercise's, not any current programme's; check current docs for real criteria. Bookings, cancellations (with who cancelled and why), messages, reviews and exception decisions are in the warehouse with event times.
sections.criteria: Versioned metric definitions owned and shared by the progress view and the assessment; a clear cut-off rule for late inputs (reviews, exceptions), announced to hosts; immutable, reproducible assessment records with counted input ids and supersession for appeals and corrections; status history queryable as of any date; publication as one atomic switch (a published assessment version) that the badge and the search benefit both read; manual overrides as recorded inputs that survive recomputation; explanations a host can follow; checks that compare the assessment with its consumers; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Does a cancellation by the guest count against the host?
clarifications.a: No. Only cancellations by the host, or by the platform because of the host, count.

clarifications.q: Which reviews count for a stay that ended on the quarter's last day?
clarifications.a: Your call. The review window is still open at the assessment date; say what you do and how hosts learn about it.

clarifications.q: What if a host has fewer than {{min_stays}} stays?
clarifications.a: They do not meet the standard this quarter, and their progress view should say so plainly.

clarifications.q: Can definitions change mid-year?
clarifications.a: Yes, with notice. An assessment always records which version it used.

clarifications.q: Does a co-host share the host's status?
clarifications.a: Status is per host account; listings managed by several hosts are counted for the primary host in this exercise.

hints: Write each assessment as an immutable record: host, quarter, definition version, data cut-off, metric values, the ids of the counted inputs, and the result. Corrections are new versions that point to the old one.
A daily progress view and the quarterly assessment should run the same definitions on different cut-offs, not two codebases.

Late inputs need a rule decided in advance: either an assessment uses only what was known at the cut-off and late inputs count next time, or late inputs trigger a re-assessment. Both are defensible; mixing them is not.
followups: Show the tables for metric definitions, assessments and status history, and the query that answers "what status did host H have on date D, and why?"
A booking was altered twice and then cancelled by the host after the guest asked to change dates. Is it a host cancellation, and how does your definition decide?
An extenuating-circumstance decision is approved three weeks after publication and would change 9,000 hosts' results. What runs, what changes for them, and what do they see?
How do you make sure the badge on listings and the search benefit switch at the publication moment and match the assessment exactly?
A definition change moves the cancellation threshold. How do you show hosts their progress under the new rule before it applies, and compare quarters fairly?

rules.ask: You re-run last quarter after an appeal and the output overwrites the table. How does a host, or support, see what the result was before the appeal and why it changed?
Reviews for stays near the quarter's end arrive after your cut-off. Do they count this quarter or next, and how does the host know which?
The daily progress view says a host meets the standard; the quarterly assessment says they do not. What are the possible causes in your design, and how do you prevent them?
Support manually overrides a result after an appeal. How does that override survive the next recomputation, and who can see it was manual?
How exactly is the overall rating computed: per review, per stay, rounded when? Show a host at 4.795 and say whether they pass.

incidents: A definition bug counts guest-requested date changes that end in a host-confirmed cancellation as host cancellations. After publication, 4% of hosts lose the badge, and appeals pile up faster than they can be handled within {{appeal_days}} days.

Reviews for stays that ended in the last two weeks of the quarter arrive after the cut-off; hosts complain that a poor review "counted in the wrong quarter", and support gives different answers to different hosts.
Severe weather closes a region and causes mass host cancellations. The extenuating-circumstances decision covering them is approved three weeks after the assessment was published.

The search benefit is switched on from a copy of the assessment taken before a late correction run; for two days, 11,000 hosts who no longer meet the standard keep the benefit and 3,000 who now meet it do not get it.

templates.title: Planning when a sudden demand shock makes historical data stop predicting
templates.subtopic: broken forecasts, scenarios, communicating confidence

shock: travel restrictions that cancel most cross-border trips within two weeks
a natural disaster that closes a popular region at the start of its peak season
a sudden shift in what guests book: far fewer city weekends, many more long stays in the countryside
consumer: the price suggestions offered to hosts
the staffing plan for customer support

sections.scenario: Your team owns the demand forecasts for a stays marketplace: nights booked and cancellations per market and stay date. They feed {{consumer}} and several other plans, some of which read them automatically every day. After {{shock}}, cancellations spike, new bookings fall in some markets and rise in others, and forecasts trained on several years of history are wrong by far more than their stated error. Leadership asks you for a demand plan for {{horizon}}, {{deadline}}.
sections.problem: What do you do? Cover the first hours (what you stop, whom you tell and what you tell them), how you produce numbers people can plan with when history no longer predicts, how you express uncertainty so that leaders use it rather than ignore it, what you change in the models and the pipeline, how you decide when to trust the models again, and what your team stops doing to make room. Then tell me about a real time a model, forecast or dashboard you owned stopped describing reality, with what happened, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: You cannot wait for months of new data. You do not own the systems that consume the forecast. Your team has other committed work this quarter.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Acts first to stop harm (automated consumers moved to a safe fallback, owners told plainly what is broken and since when); replaces a single forecast with explicit scenarios tied to assumptions and leading indicators; communicates uncertainty in a form leaders can plan with (ranges, triggers, decisions that hold across scenarios); shortens feedback loops and publishes forecast error; changes the models deliberately (shorter horizons, recent-signal features, treatment of the shock period) and sets criteria for trusting them again; makes room by stopping lower-value work; real example with what happened and personal contribution, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Does anything act on the forecast automatically?
clarifications.a: Yes. {{consumer}} reads it every day without a person in the loop.

clarifications.q: Is there a historical analogue?
clarifications.a: Partial ones: smaller regional events in past years, none at this scale.

clarifications.q: What does leadership want?
clarifications.a: Something they can plan with. They will accept ranges if they understand them.

clarifications.q: Who decides what each plan does with the numbers?
clarifications.a: Each plan's owner. You own the forecast and what you say about its quality.

hints: First stop automated decisions from acting on a forecast you know is wrong, and tell each owner plainly what is broken, since when and what you recommend instead.

Replace one number with a few explicit scenarios, each with its assumptions and the leading indicators (searches, booking pace at short lead times, cancellation rates) that would show which one is unfolding.
Shorten the feedback loop: forecast short horizons from current signals, and publish the forecast's error every week against what actually happened.
followups: What do you tell the owner of {{consumer}} in the first hour, and what do you ask them to do?
Walk me through the scenarios you would present for {{horizon}}: what differs between them, and which signals tell them apart early?
Finance says it needs one number, not three scenarios. What do you give them, and how do you make sure the other scenarios still shape decisions?
Some months later, forecast error is back to normal in most markets. How do you decide to trust the models again, and what do you do with the shock period in the training data?
In your real example, what did you get wrong first, and how did you find out?

rules.ask: Retrain on what? You have two weeks of data after the shock and years from before it. What would the new model know that the old one did not?
Leadership picks the middle scenario and plans only for it. What do you do to keep the other scenarios alive in their decisions?
Your intervals were calibrated on history that no longer applies. How do you know they are honest now?
Turning off the forecast feed leaves {{consumer}} with what instead, and who decides that?
Which call did you personally make, and what did it cost?

templates.title: A change that is good for guests and costly for hosts
templates.subtopic: two-sided trade-offs, experiment validity, fair framing of a decision

change: showing guests the full total price, fees included, from the first search page
making this exercise's more flexible cancellation rule the default for new listings
giving more search prominence to listings that can be booked instantly, without host approval
result: guest bookings up 3%, and average host earnings down 2% in the test
guest conversion up 4%, with a quarter of hosts, mostly small ones, losing bookings while the rest gain
guest satisfaction up, with more host cancellations and fewer new listings in the test period
role: the data lead who owns the experimentation platform and its metrics
the tech lead of the guest team that built the change
a staff engineer who works with both teams

sections.scenario: The guest team tested {{change}}. The three-week test shows {{result}}. The guest team wants to launch to everyone. The host team says the change hurts hosts and will shrink supply over the following months, which will hurt guests later. Each team's goals are tied to its own metrics. You are {{role}}, and both team leads have asked you to "settle it with data" before the quarterly planning meeting in two weeks.
sections.problem: What do you do? Cover how you check whether the test measures what each side claims, what it cannot show in three weeks, how you frame the decision so that both sides' effects are visible in one place, what alternatives you would put on the table, who decides and how you present to them, and how you keep both teams' trust whichever way it goes. Then tell me about a real time two teams you worked with had conflicting goals and you helped reach a decision, with what happened, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: You do not make the launch decision. Both teams must be able to trust your analysis. The planning meeting date does not move.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Examines the test's validity before arguing from it (interference between guests sharing supply, short duration, who was affected); separates what the data shows from what it cannot show yet; frames the decision with both sides' effects and guardrails agreed in advance, and with long-run supply effects as scenarios; offers alternatives (targeting, phasing, compensating changes, a market-level test); respects the decider and presents both cases fairly; supports the decision with monitoring and a rollback condition; real example with what happened and personal contribution, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: How was the test randomised?
clarifications.a: By guest. Treated and control guests booked from the same listings in the same markets.

clarifications.q: Is there a marketplace goal both teams share?
clarifications.a: Not in writing. Leadership talks about healthy growth for both sides.

clarifications.q: Who makes the call?
clarifications.a: The product leader over both teams, at the planning meeting.

clarifications.q: Can another test be run?
clarifications.a: Yes, but a test randomised by market would take at least six weeks.

hints: Check the measurement first. When treated and control guests compete for the same listings, a treated guest's booking can be a control guest's lost booking; both the guest gain and the host effect can be biased.
Put both sides' effects in one view with guardrails agreed before anyone argues from the result, and show the long-run supply effect as a range of scenarios rather than a certainty.
Look for a version that keeps most of the guest gain at a smaller host cost: targeting, phasing, or a compensating change for the hosts most affected.
followups: What, exactly, is right or wrong about this test's design for the question being asked, and how would you measure the host effect properly?
How do you estimate a supply effect that will take months to appear?
Each lead asks you privately to present the results their way. What do you do?
The product leader decides to launch. What do you put in place for the following months?
In your real example, how did you keep both sides' trust, and what would you do differently?

rules.ask: Which metric, exactly, and how do you stop it from hiding a large loss for a small group of hosts?
Which guardrail would block this launch today, and who agreed its threshold before the result was known?
That test needs at least six weeks and the planning meeting is in two. What do you say at the meeting?
What do you put in front of the product leader, and how do both leads know you presented their case fairly?
What did you personally do or say, and when?

templates.title: From a queue of one-off analysis requests to self-serve
templates.subtopic: intake, certified datasets, enabling other teams

requesters: product managers on the guest and host teams

sections.scenario: Your data team of {{team}} receives about {{requests}} one-off analysis requests a month, mostly from {{requesters}}: occupancy in one city last summer, how many hosts cancelled after a policy change, conversion by device for a new search filter. The backlog is {{backlog}}, the team does little else, and the same questions are answered several times a quarter with slightly different numbers. Your manager asks you to move the team to self-serve within two quarters, without leaving the people who depend on you stranded.
sections.problem: How would you lead the change? Cover how you find out which requests repeat and why, what you build first (datasets, definitions, tools), how you keep self-serve numbers correct and consistent, how requesters learn to use it, what happens to new requests during the transition and after it, how you bring your team along, and how you measure whether it worked. Then tell me about a real time you changed how a team worked with the people it served, with what happened, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: No extra headcount. Requesters' skills range from SQL to spreadsheets. Some requests are urgent and come from executives. Self-serve must never expose an individual guest's or host's personal data.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Starts from evidence (classified past requests, repeat questions, where numbers disagreed); builds a small set of certified, documented datasets and definitions with owners, booking-date and stay-date versions made explicit, before tools; protects personal data by design (aggregates, access controls); a published intake policy with a fast lane; teaches requesters and checks they get correct answers; brings the team along with new roles (owning definitions, harder analysis); measures outcomes (repeat questions answered without the team, consistency of numbers, time to answer, team time freed); real example with what happened and personal contribution, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Do requesters write SQL?
clarifications.a: A few do; most use spreadsheets and dashboards.

clarifications.q: Are there dashboards already?
clarifications.a: Dozens, many abandoned, with conflicting definitions of the same metric.

clarifications.q: Can the team say no to requests?
clarifications.a: Your manager will back a published intake policy, not case-by-case refusals.

clarifications.q: How does the team feel about it?
clarifications.a: Tired of the queue, but some enjoy the analysis work and worry it will disappear.

hints: Classify a quarter of past requests; a handful of question types usually covers most of them, and the rest tells you what self-serve will not do.
The product is a small set of certified datasets and metric definitions with owners and documentation, not more dashboards. Decide which date each metric uses (booking date or stay date) and say so.
Keep a fast lane for questions self-serve cannot answer, with a published policy for what qualifies.
followups: How do you choose the first three things to build, and what evidence do you use?
Operations and finance both ask for "occupancy" and mean different things. What do you build, and who decides the definition?
Six weeks in, requests have not fallen: people use the new datasets but still ask your team to check their numbers. What do you change?
How do you measure whether self-serve works, beyond fewer tickets?
In your real example, what did the people you served resist, and how did you respond?

rules.ask: There are already dozens of abandoned dashboards. Why will yours be used, and who retires the old ones?
Who still attends after the first month, and how do you know they can answer their own questions correctly?
A requester joins a certified dataset to their own spreadsheet and a wrong number reaches an executive. Whose problem is it, and what do you change?
An executive's urgent request arrives the week after you stopped taking one-off work. What happens?
Which parts did you personally design or decide?

templates.title: Making an untested critical pipeline safe to change without a freeze
templates.subtopic: safety nets for legacy pipelines, persuading leadership, adoption across teams

pipeline: the host payout calculation that feeds the payments system
the nightly bookings and revenue tables that finance closes the books on
the features that search ranking uses
incident: last month a change double-counted cleaning fees for a day before anyone noticed
a renamed column silently zeroed one of its outputs for a week
a time-zone fix moved a day of bookings into the wrong month

sections.scenario: You have just taken over the pipeline behind {{pipeline}}. It has almost no tests, {{teams}} teams change it about {{changes}} times a week, and {{incident}}. After that incident a director proposes freezing all changes for a quarter while the pipeline is rewritten. You think a freeze would stall the teams that depend on changing it, and that a rewrite carries its own risk. You are asked for an alternative plan by next week.
sections.problem: What do you propose, and how do you lead it? Cover what makes changes safer quickly when nobody fully understands the code, what you do first and why, how changes are reviewed, tested and released from now on, how you get {{teams}} teams to adopt it, how you convince the director that your plan is safer than a freeze, and how you show over the following months that risk has actually fallen. Then tell me about a real time you made a fragile system safe to change, with what happened, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: No general freeze. No extra headcount this quarter. The pipeline's outputs reach money, the books or what guests see.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Proposes fast safety nets that do not need full understanding (shadow runs with output comparison on production inputs, characterisation tests from real data, blocking output checks and reconciliations), ordered by which past incidents they would have caught; makes changes reversible (versioned outputs, re-runs, quick rollback); sets a change process with clear ownership and handling of intended differences; adopts it with the teams rather than imposing it; persuades the director with evidence and a clear risk comparison, possibly accepting a narrow freeze; measures results (escaped defects, time to detect, change lead time); real example with what happened and personal contribution, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Does anyone understand the whole pipeline?
clarifications.a: Pieces of it, spread across the teams. The original author has left.

clarifications.q: Can it be run twice side by side?
clarifications.a: Yes, at roughly double the compute cost for that run.

clarifications.q: How was the last incident found?
clarifications.a: Someone downstream noticed a number that looked wrong.

clarifications.q: Is there a staging environment?
clarifications.a: A staging copy exists, but its data is months old and a small sample.

hints: You cannot quickly write unit tests for behaviour nobody can specify, but you can pin today's behaviour: run the old and new code on the same production inputs and compare the outputs before a change is released.
Add checks on the outputs that block publication rather than only alert: totals that reconcile with the sources, no duplicated rows, values inside expected ranges.
Make every change reversible: versioned outputs, the ability to re-run a day, and a rollback measured in minutes.
followups: What do you put in place in the first two weeks, and which of the past incidents would it have caught?
A team's change is meant to alter the output, and your comparison blocks it. How does the process handle intended differences?
How do you convince the director that your plan is safer than a freeze?
Two months in, what do you measure to show that risk is lower?
In your real example, what did you have to slow down or stop, and who objected?

rules.ask: Nobody can say what the code should do in its corner cases. What are your unit tests asserting, and how do you know those assertions are right?
The rewrite takes two quarters while {{changes}} changes a week keep landing on the old code. How do the two stay in step?
The comparison shows 0.3% of rows differ on every run even with no code change. What do you do before anyone trusts it?
The director agrees to drop the general freeze but insists on one for the riskiest part. Do you accept, and on what terms?
What did you personally do or decide?

templates.title: Project deep dive, re-examined for a two-sided marketplace of hosts and guests
templates.subtopic: design decisions, failures, two-sided marketplace data

angle: the data model and how it handled change
the hardest correctness problem you solved
the decision you would make differently today
two_sided: metrics where a gain for one side can be a loss for the other
experiments in which treated and control users compete for the same supply
data both sides see, where each side may see only its own part
lag: outcomes that arrive months after the event that caused them, such as a stay booked long before it happens
facts that change after the event, such as alterations, cancellations and partial refunds

sections.scenario: In this part of the loop you describe a data system you designed or substantially changed, one that other teams or customers depended on. The interviewer will go deep on {{angle}}, then ask how the system would have to change to serve a two-sided marketplace of hosts and guests, where it must handle {{two_sided}} and {{lag}}.
sections.problem: Give a five-minute overview: the problem, the users, the scale in numbers, the architecture and your role. Then go deep on {{angle}}. Then reason through what would change if the system served a marketplace with hosts on one side and guests on the other, with {{two_sided}} and {{lag}}. If you have never owned such a system, say so, pick the closest thing you have worked on, and be clear about which parts you are reasoning through rather than recalling.
sections.constraints: Your own project only. Describe it without revealing anything a previous employer would not want shared; round numbers are fine if you say so.
sections.assumptions: The marketplace setting is hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Clear problem framing with real numbers; depth on the chosen angle down to keys, schemas and failure modes; decisions explained with alternatives and evidence; honest account of what broke and what changed; a credible marketplace analysis (both sides' views of one event, interference between competing users, access limited to each side's own data) tied to the candidate's own system; a concrete approach to late or changing facts (event dates versus effective dates, restatements, versioned outputs); own contribution clearly separated from the team's, or an honest statement of reasoning rather than recall.

clarifications.q: Does it have to be a marketplace system?
clarifications.a: No. Any system with real users works; the second half asks what would change.

clarifications.q: Can it be a team project?
clarifications.a: Yes, but separate what you did from what the team did.

clarifications.q: How deep should I go?
clarifications.a: Down to schemas, keys, failure modes and numbers.

hints: Lead with the problem and the numbers before the architecture.
Have one decision you would defend again and one you would change.
For the marketplace question, say which of your tables or metrics would describe only one side, and what the other side's view of the same event would be.
followups: What was the main alternative to your key design decision, and what evidence chose between them?
What broke in production, how did you find out, and what did you change?
